Validated at the boundary by `PendingCommitmentSchema` (`lib/schemas/guest-commitment.ts`). Write sites: `lib/agent/schedule-and-send.ts` `buildOutboundInsert` / `persistOrRegenQueuedDraft` (INSERT writes the carrier; regen UPDATE OVERWRITES wholesale so the carrier always reflects the current draft). Read site: `lib/operator/dispatch-operator-outbound.ts` extends its first SELECT to include the column, then after the second UPDATE stamps `status='sent'`, calls `createCommitmentFromPending` to materialize. Rejected / skipped draft → never dispatched → no row (per the "create on send, not at draft" invariant). **TAC-385 PR 1 adds a second read of the same shape**: `messages.rendered_intentions` (migration 045) comes back in the same SELECT, and a step 8 after the commitment materialization fires `recordIntentionPrompts` via `waitUntil` with the DISPATCHED body, so an approved or edited send records the ask the auto-send path already records. Fire-and-forget rather than awaited, unlike step 7: it is a Haiku call on the operator's approve tap, and the message has already gone out, so a recording failure must never turn a successful dispatch into a 502. The ungated rec path (auto-send via `scheduleAndSend`) writes the row inline post-dispatch rather than using the carrier — no queue gap to bridge. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`)** — per *Database migrations* §"Ordering for backwards-incompatible migrations": additive shape but the deployed code SELECTs the new column, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging the PR**. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. TAC-297.
- `028_venue_configs_followup_rules.sql` — adds `venue_configs.followup_rules jsonb` (nullable at the storage layer for migration ordering safety; `parseFollowupRules` in `lib/schemas/followup-rules.ts` fills in defaults on null/missing). Backs the TAC-123 follow-up engine. Backfills a versioned default literal for every existing row in the same migration (kept in sync with `FOLLOWUP_RULES_DEFAULT` — round-tripped in `followup-rules.test.ts` to lock the invariant). Bumps `venue_configs.schema_version` from 1 → 2 (the column has existed since migration 001 — this is the first non-1 value). Pre-existing `venue_configs.messaging_cadence` stays the pure day-schedule (`{day_1, day_3, day_7, day_14}`); the new `followup_rules` carries everything else (gates, weekly cap, quiet hours, cron hour, per-reason kill switches, lapsed-eligible states, dedup windows). **Backwards-incompatible per the deploy-ordering rule** — the deployed code SELECTs the new column on read (`lib/followups/engine.ts`), so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging the PR**. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. TAC-123.
- `029_create_followup_log.sql` — creates `followup_log` table for TAC-123's per-reason dispatch audit + claim-before-side-effect idempotency. Columns: `id`, `venue_id`, `guest_id`, `reason` (CHECK-constrained closed enum matching `FOLLOWUP_REASONS` in `lib/schemas/followup-rules.ts`), `dedup_key text` (reason-appropriate: `day_N:<last_visit_at_iso>` / `cold:<last_visit_at_iso>` / `perk:<mechanic_id>` per `dedupKeyForReason`), nullable `message_id` (filled in by `finalizeFollowupLogClaim` post-dispatch — multi-reason runs share one message_id as the run correlator), `created_at`. Three indexes: UNIQUE on `(venue_id, guest_id, dedup_key)` (load-bearing — claim conflicts return `23505`); `(venue_id, guest_id, created_at desc)` (weekly-cap query); `(venue_id, guest_id, reason, created_at desc)` (per-reason last-dispatch lookup). Claim flow per engine run is: INSERT (`claimFollowupLogRows`) → handleFollowup → on `sent`/`queued` UPDATE message_id (`finalizeFollowupLogClaim`) → on `refused`/`failed` DELETE the claim (`releaseFollowupLogClaim`) so dedup isn't burned. Append-only — no `updated_at`. Additive but the deployed code INSERTs on engine tick, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging the PR**. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit. TAC-123.

- `030_square_integration.sql` — **Backfilled by TAC-323** (previously landed undocumented; flagged for whoever next touched the Square integration). Builds on the mock-first `transactions` table from migration 001 (`guest_id` nullable-until-matched, `source` check already containing `'square'`/`'toast'` from day one) — adds the columns + tables real Square ingestion needs without redesigning the transactions model. Six pieces: (1) `transactions.card_fingerprint` — Square's stable, non-PCI card fingerprint, plus a partial index and two new `match_method` values (`card_fingerprint`, `tap_time_window`) alongside the migration-001 set. (2) `guest_card_fingerprints` — per-venue fingerprint→guest map (matches the `guests UNIQUE(venue_id, phone_number)` isolation decision); first tap writes the mapping, every later transaction with that fingerprint auto-resolves the guest with no tap required. (3) `pos_credentials` — OAuth-ready per-venue-per-provider Square/Toast/Clover credentials, tokens app-layer encrypted (`lib/pos/crypto.ts`), never plaintext. (4) `pos_catalog_items` + (5) `pos_inventory_counts` — mirror of the venue's Square catalog + best-effort inventory, refreshed on backfill and `catalog.version.updated` webhooks. (6) `pos_webhook_events` — dedupes Square webhook deliveries (which can repeat/arrive out of order) on the provider's `event_id`, covering non-transaction events the `transactions` unique constraint doesn't reach. Plus `pos_tap_events` (NFC tap opt-in: a tap opens iMessage with a server-issued `tap_token`; the reconciler matches a pending tap to a Square transaction by location + nearest timestamp) and `pos_devices` (the wifi-connected eink/Arduino display side, bearer-token-authenticated, storing only its sha256 hash). Additive only — standard-care migration, not on the high-stakes table list; the companion Square webhook handler is the payment-adjacent high-stakes surface, flagged separately. No Linear ticket on record for the original migration.
- `031_venue_hold_all_outbound.sql` — adds `venues.hold_all_outbound boolean not null default false`. Per-venue blanket hold: when true, `applyApprovalPolicyStage` fires the `hold_all_outbound` trigger (#6) and queues every guest-facing content message for operator review, EXCEPT `opt_out` confirmations (TCPA/carrier compliance — those must auto-send). Read by `build-runtime-context.ts` into `VenueContext.holdAllOutbound`; ranked last in `PRIMARY_TRIGGER_PRIORITY`. **No UI, no API, no seed default writes this column** — every `from('venues')` call in the repo is a `.select()`. Flip it by hand in Studio (template in Common gotchas). Additive; existing rows covered by the DEFAULT. Shipped in commit `0c1515c` with `TAC-XXX` placeholders and no Linear ticket — the placeholders remain in `lib/agent/stages.ts`, `lib/operator/queue.ts`, and the migration header.

- `032_message_splitting_generation_id.sql` — TAC-313 message splitting. Adds `messages.generation_id uuid` (nullable) + partial index `idx_messages_generation_id WHERE generation_id IS NOT NULL` — the key that groups the rows of one agent response when a reply is dispatched as multiple Sendblue messages. **One row per bubble is forced by evidence:** the Sendblue status webhook looks up rows by `provider_message_id` and each send returns its own handle, so one row for two bubbles leaves the second bubble's delivery status with nowhere to land. Minted fresh per dispatch in `scheduleAndSend` — deliberately NOT `agentRunId`, since the Langfuse link already lives on `langfuse_trace_id` and coupling them would silently merge two responses into one group if a run ever dispatched twice. Plain indexed uuid, NOT a self-FK: a self-FK leaves the first bubble null and forces a null special case at every read site. **Drops `messages.parent_draft_id`** (dead since migration 001 — indexed self-FK, zero readers, zero writers) so it can't sit beside `generation_id` as a second plausible grouping column; not reused either, because a column named `parent_draft_id` holding generation grouping is a naming lie. **NO BACKFILL, deliberately** — every consumer uses the grouping identity `coalesce(generation_id, id)`, so legacy rows, inbound rows, single-bubble replies and queue drafts are each their own group via their own PK. That expression is what makes the three call sites (the two functions below and the TS projection in `build-runtime-context.ts`) agree by construction rather than by discipline. Adds `count_outbound_responses(p_venue_id, p_guest_id)` — `count(distinct coalesce(generation_id, id))` over sent/delivered outbound, consumed by `lib/recognition/load-signals.ts`; without it splitting inflates the `responseRate = replied / sent` **denominator only** (weight 0.10 in `computeRelationshipStrength`) and guests drift downward out of `regular` with no change in behavior. Replaces `list_operator_queue` (migration 018) — only the `ctx` lateral changes: `recent_context` now groups by response and returns the 3 most recent RESPONSES, **merged into ≤3 entries** (id = first bubble's real id, body = bubbles space-joined + `btrim`, createdAt = `min(created_at)`) rather than returning up to 9 bubble rows, because `QueueRecentContextEntry` is a cross-repo shape and widening its cardinality while multi-bubble card rendering is out of scope would be a silent Contract change. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`).** Contains a `DROP COLUMN` but applies in Studio **BEFORE** merge per the inert-drop exception documented above under §"Ordering for backwards-incompatible migrations". db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. TAC-313.

- `034_guest_enrollment_and_self_reported_orders.sql` — TAC-323: guest enrollment via a static QR sign (at pickup, not the register — so there's no transaction to check the guest into) plus self-reported orders (the guest texts back what they got; the venue has no POS record to attach it to). Three changes: (1) `transactions.source` check gains `'guest_reported'`. (2) `transactions.amount_cents` becomes nullable — reserved for the one case where a resolved item has no price in `venue_info`; the WHOLE order's amount is null rather than a partial sum, because a partial sum looks complete and isn't. Every `amount_cents` consumer was audited for this null path in the same PR: `lib/recognition/load-signals.ts` (`totalSpentCents += amount_cents ?? 0` — SUM-ignores-NULL semantics, not a claim the order cost $0), the admin conversations page (`pricedVisitCount90d` excludes null-amount rows from the avg-per-visit denominator so one unpriced order can't drag the average down, while still counting as a visit), and `transaction-row.tsx` (renders a muted "—", never a fabricated "$0.00"). (3) `guests.created_via` gains `'qr_scan'`, same drop-and-recreate pattern as migration 006. Plus one new partial unique index, `idx_transactions_one_guest_reported_per_guest` on `(venue_id, guest_id) where source='guest_reported'` — closes a TOCTOU race between two near-simultaneous inbounds from the same guest each independently naming a menu item, same rationale and shape as migration 020's `idx_messages_one_pending_per_guest` (TAC-264); a `23505` on insert is treated the same as the ordinary "already reported" outcome (log, no throw, no red alert). **No new `venue_configs` column** — the QR sign's expected prefilled-message string lives as a new optional `qrEnrollmentMessage` field on the EXISTING `venue_info` jsonb (`lib/schemas/venue-info.ts`), not a new column; a bare new column was the original draft and was pushed back on during plan review as an unscoped schema change outside the repo's per-venue-config-with-a-Zod-schema convention. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `transactions` and `guests`)** — additive shape (per CLAUDE.md's own §Ordering, "order doesn't matter" for new enum values + a relaxed NOT NULL + a new index), so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merging this PR — a deviation from this ticket's original "deploy code first" call, which only reasoned about the qr_scan half (gated by the sign not being printed yet); the self-reported-orders half has no such gate, so applying after merge would open a real window where an existing guest's self-report hits the pre-migration constraints and is silently, permanently lost. See the migration file's own header for the full reasoning. Constraint names (`transactions_source_check`, `guests_created_via_check`) verified against this migration's own history, not assumed — re-verify against live `pg_constraint` immediately before applying in Studio per the standing caution on this table. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit (`transactions.amount_cents` → `number | null`) until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply.

- `035_guest_intention_prompts.sql` — TAC-324: first-touch intentions. Creates `guest_intention_prompts` (id, venue_id, guest_id, intention_key, message_id nullable + ON DELETE SET NULL, prompted_at, created_at) with a UNIQUE constraint on `(guest_id, intention_key)` — the storage-layer cap: one prompt per intention per guest, ever, enforced by the database rather than application logic. Satisfaction is deliberately NOT stored here (derived live from `transactions` at context-build time — see `lib/agent/intentions/derive.ts`); this table exists only because "Sana asked and the guest changed the subject" leaves no trace anywhere else. Deliberately NOT `engagement_events` — that table feeds `ENGAGEMENT_EVENT_WEIGHTS`, and raising a topic is not a guest action that should move the recognition formula. Additive, new table, not on the standing high-stakes list, but per the `guest_commitments` (026) / `followup_log` (029) precedent, deployed code both SELECTs and INSERTs into it on the very next qr_scan guest's inbound after deploy, so apply in Studio BEFORE merging the PR, same reasoning as those two. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply.

- `036_visit_time_precision.sql` — TAC-377: two nullable `text` columns with CHECK constraints, `transactions.occurred_at_precision` and `guests.last_visit_precision`, both `'pinned' | 'approximate'`. Backs self-reported visits advancing `guests.last_visit_at` — before this, that column was written ONLY by the two Square paths, so at a venue with no POS integration every guest had `last_visit_at = null`, `detectPostVisitReason` and `detectColdLapsedReason` both returned null forever, and the hourly follow-up cron ran, scanned, reported success, and could not fire. **`transactions.occurred_at_precision` has NO reader in app code today** — it is written by `extract-reported-order.ts` and read by nothing; `guests.last_visit_precision` is written independently in the same function rather than derived from it. Stated rather than left to be discovered, per the `approval_policy`-went-102-days-unread lesson: it is per-transaction provenance kept so a future visit-history surface (or a backfill of `last_visit_precision` after a `guest_reported` row is deleted) has something to read. **No backfill, deliberately** — null means "nobody recorded a precision," which is honestly different from either value, and the detector reads null as PERMISSIVE (see the followup-engine section). Both are NEW names on NEW columns, so unlike migration 034 there is no drop-and-recreate and no constraint-name drift to verify — `add constraint` fails loudly if a name somehow already exists. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `transactions`)** — additive shape, but deployed code SELECTs both columns, so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merging the PR, same call 034 made on this table. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply.

- `037_guest_commitments_open_dedup.sql` — TAC-318: partial unique index `guest_commitments_open_dedup` on `(venue_id, guest_id, lower(trim(both from description))) WHERE status = 'open'`. At most one OPEN commitment per guest per description. **Applied in Studio ahead of the migration file, together with a hand-collapse of the existing duplicates** (fleet 9 → 7 rows; Le Mil's left with one Blossom Tonic and one SoFi) — the file is the repo-side record, since `db/migrations` is the single source of DB truth. Three things about the key are decisions, not defaults. **`type` is deliberately NOT in it**: two open promises with the same description are the same promise to the guest whatever the agent labelled them, and a type-scoped key would let one turn's `recommendation: cortado` sit beside a later turn's `comp: cortado` as two live entries in the same prompt block. **`lower(trim(...))` is a FUNCTIONAL index expression**, mirrored in JS by `commitmentDedupKey` (`lib/guests/commitments.ts`) — the two must move together; they are not byte-identical (Postgres `trim(both from)` strips spaces only, JS `.trim()` strips all whitespace) and do not need to be, because both layers are present and each divergence direction degrades safely. **`WHERE status = 'open'` excludes `pending_ack`**, deliberately narrower than the `## Active commitments` block's own open+pending_ack filter: once the guest has signalled arrival the row is mid-flight against a specific visit, so a later promise is genuinely new. Terminal states sit outside the index, so in principle a comp redeemed in March can be promised again in June — **but do not read that as a live escape valve, because two of those states have no writer.** Nothing in this repo ever sets `guest_commitments.status` to `'expired'` or `'redeemed'` (enum values in the schema, zero writers), and `guest_commitments.expires_at` is write-only — set on insert, read by nothing. **SUPERSEDED IN PART BY TAC-341 (migration 038): `expired` now has a writer and `expires_at` now has both a server-side derivation and a reader.** `redeemed` still has none — it ships with its caller in TAC-378. Read the two paragraphs that follow as history: for OBLIGATIONS (comp/hold/discount) a row now does leave `open`, so the dedup on that description is no longer permanent. For `recommendation` every word of them still holds, because TAC-341 deliberately excluded that type — TAC-380 owns it. The only transitions that exist are `open → pending_ack` and `pending_ack → acknowledged | cancelled`, all requiring the guest to signal arrival. **Consequence, which is a product fact rather than a doc nit: for `recommendation` — the whole population this ticket is about, the type that never gates, never carries a code, and that guests rarely signal arrival against — a row enters `open` and effectively never leaves, so the dedup on that description is PERMANENT for the life of the guest's relationship with that venue.** A guest recommended the Blossom Tonic in September can never be recommended it again, and the block renders it as "promised 6 months ago" indefinitely. Right for this ticket's brief, wrong as a steady state; TAC-341 builds the `expired`/`redeemed` writers and sets the horizons, which is what turns the first sentence from principle into fact. Caught in code review, not in the plan. **The app-level check is the PRIMARY enforcement, not this index** — see the runtime-contract entry. Additive (index only), no column, no backfill; indexes don't surface in generated types so `db/types.ts` is unchanged. Standard-care — `guest_commitments` is not on the high-stakes table list. Ordering doesn't matter: deployed code tolerates the index's absence (app check alone) and its presence (the 23505 branch).
- `038_guest_commitments_escalated_at.sql` — TAC-341: one nullable `escalated_at timestamptz` on `guest_commitments`, plus partial index `idx_guest_commitments_expiry` on `(expires_at) WHERE status='open' AND expires_at IS NOT NULL` (sibling of 026's `idx_guest_commitments_due`, different column — that one serves the arrival cron's `expected_arrival` scan, this one the lifecycle cron's). **The status enum is UNCHANGED and that is the point**: migration 026 already permitted all six of `open`/`pending_ack`/`acknowledged`/`redeemed`/`expired`/`cancelled`, and `expired` had simply never been written by anything. The ticket's own AC said "no migration was required" and that was **right about the enum and wrong about escalation** — escalation needs durable state or it is not idempotent, and the hourly cron would re-fire the same Slack alert on every tick for the whole window between escalation and expiry. **The original figure was ~17,000 alerts for one comp, computed against the 2-year horizon this ticket shipped with; the horizon became 60 days the same day, so the live number is ~1,272** (53 open days past the 7-day window, hourly). Recomputed rather than left standing, because a stale justification number is how a decision stops being re-derivable — and the conclusion is unchanged at either figure. That does not make the alert noisy, it makes it worthless, which is the `comp_regex_backstop` illusion in a new costume. **`escalated_at` is an IDEMPOTENCY MARKER, not an audit trail** — it answers exactly one question (has a human been told) and the REASON rides on the `commitment_escalated` PostHog event instead; resisting `escalated_reason`/`escalation_count` columns is what keeps it honest about its one job. **Deliberately NOT a seventh status**: `'escalated'` would have taken the row OUT of `'open'`, which is the filter every other consumer keys on (`findActiveCommitmentsForGuest`, the `## Active commitments` block, 037's open-dedup index) — an escalated commitment is still open and still owed, so escalation is a notification fact about the row, not a lifecycle state of the promise. The index is deliberately NOT filtered on `type`: the scan restricts to obligations in app code, but baking a `recommendation` exclusion into the index would need a migration the day TAC-380 changes what a recommendation is. Additive (one nullable column, no default, no backfill, no constraint change) but deployed code SELECTs `escalated_at`, so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merge per §Ordering — same call 025/026/034/035/036 made. Standard care; `guest_commitments` is not on the high-stakes table list. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. **Companion backfill is SEPARATE SQL, applied by hand** — see the template under Common gotchas.

- `039_operator_queue_review_detail.sql` — TAC-364: two nullable `text[]` columns on `messages` (`review_triggers`, `ungrounded_claims`) plus a recreate of `list_operator_queue` returning both. `review_reason` keeps holding the priority-selected primary; `review_triggers` holds the full set the gate fired, so a comp commitment that was ALSO below the auto-send fidelity floor no longer reaches the operator labelled only "Commitment requires approval" with the second condition unrecoverable. `ungrounded_claims` carries the grounding verifier's verbatim flagged claims — **three-state, deliberately: a non-empty array is what it flagged, `[]` means the check RAN and found nothing, NULL means it DID NOT RUN** (followup, demo guest, model self-reported a gap, or a truncated unreadable verdict). That split is not incidental: TAC-367 was filed because a silently-skipped grounding check was invisible everywhere, and conflating the two would have rebuilt that blind spot in a new column on its first day. `review_triggers` needs no equivalent split — the gate returns `send` when nothing fires, so a queued draft's trigger set is never empty, and there NULL means only "no gate ran for this row". One caveat was inherited from TAC-367 and is **CLOSED by TAC-424**: a TRANSIENT verifier fault used to fail open and record as `[]`, not NULL — byte-identical to a genuine pass, which is the one thing this column exists to distinguish. It is its own `degraded` state now, maps to NULL with the other no-verdict outcomes, and holds the draft. **Historical rows are left as they are** (ruling 3 A): anything from before that ticket means "recorded before this distinction existed", and matching them against a separate failure log was considered and declined. **The LIVE `comment on column messages.ungrounded_claims` in the database still says a transient fault records `[]`, and is now wrong** — it was applied by this migration and TAC-424 shipped no migration to correct it, because ruling 1 C said no migration on `messages`. Whoever queries this column in Studio reads that comment first, so treat CLAUDE.md as the authority and fix the comment when a `messages` migration next lands for another reason. Flagged on TAC-424 rather than decided unilaterally. The claims were previously computed, sent to PostHog/Langfuse and then discarded at exactly the point they became useful — TAC-301 part 1.5 stopped blanking the body on a backstop catch, which made a one-swipe bad approval possible for the first time, and the operator had no way to know which sentence was the suspect one. `messages.response_review` was the no-migration alternative and was rejected: that column means "a human reviewed this" and `getReviewedVia` plus the cc-review/mobile-operator consumers read it on that basis. **NO BACKFILL, deliberately** — a null `review_triggers` beside a non-null `review_reason` means "recorded before this shipped" and renders as today; synthesizing a one-element array from `review_reason` would claim the primary was the ONLY trigger, which is the thing the column exists to stop assuming. **The RPC is DROPPED and recreated, not `create or replace`d** — see the gotcha below. The whole file runs in ONE transaction so no reader observes a window where the function is missing. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`)** — additive shape, but deployed code SELECTs both columns through the RPC, so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merging the PR, same call 025/026/034/035/036/038 made. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply.

- `040_intention_state_rows.sql` — TAC-380: `guest_intention_prompts` becomes one STATE row per (guest, intention). `prompted_at` drops NOT NULL (null = eligible, not yet raised) but **KEEPS its `DEFAULT now()`** — the deployed pre-TAC-380 recorder omits the column and relies on the default, so dropping it before deploy would store every window-period prompt as null, which new code reads as unasked and re-asks. Drop it in a follow-up migration after deploy (TAC-392). Adds `eligible_at timestamptz` (the expiry anchor) and `prompt_source text CHECK in ('classified','pessimistic')` (so the brake can exclude closures that asked nothing), plus `venue_configs.intention_rules jsonb` (nullable; `parseIntentionRules` fails open to defaults). Backfill: prompted rows get `eligible_at = prompted_at` and `prompt_source = 'classified'`; `learn_first_order` renames to `understand_order`, carrying an old prompt onto a new eligibility row before deleting so the unique constraint can't abort a post-deploy re-run; `invite_contact_save` is deliberately NOT migrated (ruling 5) — the Command Center renders its orphan as unrecognized. As of 2026-09-14 that orphan is the only row fleet-wide, so the rename matches nothing today. Additive, but deployed code SELECTs the new columns, so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merge, then **re-run the backfill block (between its markers) AFTER deploy** to catch rows the old code writes in the window. Not on the high-stakes table list. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. The traps this migration creates are under Common gotchas.

- `041_two_pending_slots_per_guest.sql` — TAC-394, option F: replaces migration 020's single partial unique index with two, so a guest holds at most one pending draft PER SLOT. `idx_messages_one_pending_obligation_per_guest` covers pending rows whose `pending_commitment->>'type'` is `comp`, `hold` or `discount`; `idx_messages_one_pending_conversation_per_guest` covers every other pending row (no carrier, a recommendation, a blank knowledge-gap card). **Why:** on 2026-09-14 a pending comp draft was regenerated in place by the reply to the guest's next question, because 020 allowed one pending row and TAC-264 regenerates that row. Three choices in the file are load-bearing. **Create before drop, in one transaction**, so `messages` is never without a uniqueness constraint on pending rows; both new indexes build while 020 exists, because 020 is strictly stronger. **Not `CONCURRENTLY`**, which cannot run inside a transaction; the one-transaction swap matters more than a write lock lasting milliseconds at pilot size. **`coalesce(pending_commitment->>'type', '')`** in both predicates, because without it a NULL carrier evaluates `not in (...)` to NULL and the row matches NEITHER index. The SQL type list and `OBLIGATION_TYPES` (`lib/guests/commitment-expiry.ts`) move together, and `pending-slots.test.ts` reads this file to enforce that. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`).** Apply in Studio **BEFORE** merge, outside Le Mil's hours (7am to 3pm America/Los_Angeles): run the header's three read-only pre-checks, apply 041 then 042, merge within about two minutes, and run the header's two-card detection query once both production deploys are ready. **Roll back only when BOTH hold:** the new code is NOT live 30 minutes after applying, AND the detection query returns no rows. If it returns rows, fix forward: recreating 020 would need every guest collapsed to one pending card by hand, and the rollback transaction aborts harmlessly on the duplicate anyway. Indexes don't surface in generated types, so this file needs no `db/types.ts` change.
- `042_operator_queue_other_pending.sql` — TAC-394: drops and recreates `list_operator_queue` in one transaction (a new return column is a return-type change; see migration 039 and its gotcha), restating 039's body with two changes. It adds `other_pending_for_guest integer`, the count of OTHER pending drafts for the same venue and guest (0 or 1 under 041), projected as `QueueDraft.otherPendingDraftsForGuest`. And `recent_context` now excludes every pending row, not just the card's own, so a comp card's context never shows the conversation card's unsent draft as history (`id <> m.id` stays, for readability). **HIGH-STAKES (reads `messages`).** Apply in Studio **BEFORE** merge, immediately after 041; it can stay if 041 is rolled back, since old code ignores the extra column. Verify the live function definition before dropping, per the header. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply.
- `043_operator_conversations_reached_guest.sql` — TAC-395: `create or replace` of `list_operator_conversations` (migration 033), same signature and columns, so no `db/types.ts` change. A guest's fields now come only from messages that reached them (inbound, or outbound whose `review_state` is not pending and whose `status` is `sending`, `sent` or `delivered`), so an unsent draft can no longer be the last-message preview. A guest with no such message stays in the list (TAC-395 rulings, 21:44 and 21:55): their fields are computed from all their non-empty messages as before, and `last_message_body` is `''`. Membership, ordering and the 200-row cap are unchanged, and `body <> ''` stays where 033 had it. **HIGH-STAKES (reads `messages`).** Body-only, so it can be applied before or after merge; apply back to back with 044 and check the live definition with `pg_get_functiondef` first. `lib/operator/reached-guest-condition.test.ts` binds its status list to `DELIVERED_OUTBOUND_STATUSES`.
- `044_operator_queue_context_reached_guest.sql` — TAC-395: `create or replace` of `list_operator_queue` (migration 042), restating 042's body. The `recent_context` lateral replaces `review_state is distinct from 'pending'` with the full reached-guest condition, applied per row before grouping and before the 3-response limit, so skipped drafts and replies that never sent leave a card's context too. **No `body <> ''`, deliberately** (22:08 ruling): `recent_context` has always returned empty-body entries, and a photo-only text is context the operator needs; the binding test fails if a body filter is added. `recent_context` is already `jsonb` and no column is added, so the return type is unchanged and no DROP is needed. **HIGH-STAKES (reads `messages`).** Body-only; apply back to back with 043. It narrows what TAC-394's Contract says `recentContext` excludes; the entry shape is unchanged.
- `045_messages_rendered_intentions.sql` — TAC-385 PR 1: one nullable `jsonb` column on `messages`, `rendered_intentions`, holding the intentions RENDERED into the prompt that produced a draft as `{"key", "eligibleAt"}` entries. It is what lets `dispatchOperatorOutbound` record the ask when an operator approves or edits a card — that path recorded nothing, 13 of 34 sent replies at Le Mil's in the 30 days to 2026-09-14, and TAC-380 made it seven intentions per guest rather than two. Shaped like `pending_commitment` (027): a jsonb intent carrier on the draft row, read back at dispatch, camelCase inside the payload. **`eligibleAt` is stored rather than looked up at dispatch, and that is the load-bearing part** — `closeIntentions` guards the two event-armed intentions' stamp on `eligible_at <= anchor` AND `prompted_at IS NULL OR prompted_at < anchor`, and those two re-arm on a newer recommendation or order, so reading the guest's CURRENT anchor after a draft has sat in the queue would stamp a prompt from the OLD arming onto the NEW one. Re-deriving the whole set at dispatch is wrong for the same family of reasons (TAC-380 trap 4). NULL means "nothing rendered, or the row predates this" — both read as "record nothing" — and a blank knowledge-gap card is written NULL deliberately (ruled 2026-09-15): its dispatched text is entirely operator-authored. **NO BACKFILL, NO INDEX** (the only read is by primary key). **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`)** — additive, but deployed code SELECTs it, so apply in Studio **BEFORE** merging, same call 025/026/027/034/035/036/038/039 made. db/types.ts hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. **PR 1 does NOT change when an intention closes** — raising still closes; the asked/closed split is PR 2.
- `046_messages_status_drop_dead_default.sql` — TAC-416: drops the default on `messages.status`, which was unreachable. The column has been `not null default 'pending'` since migration 001 while `messages_status_check` has never permitted `'pending'` — both halves sit in the SAME statement in 001, on adjacent lines (318-328) — so any insert relying on the default produced a value the check immediately rejected. **Not a typo: `default 'pending'` is 001's house convention for a status column** (`venues.status` line 35, `venue_configs.onboarding_status` line 147, later `pos_tap_events.status` in 030 — all three list `'pending'` among their permitted values and are correct); `messages` copied the default and then wrote a message-lifecycle value list starting at `'received'`/`'draft'` that never included the generic opening state. **Nothing read it**, necessarily — an insert relying on it would already fail — verified across the three insert sites and the whole source tree, where every other `'pending'` literal belongs to `pos_tap_events.status`, `venues.status`, or `review_state`, each of whose constraints does permit it. **No backfill**, and the durable claim needs no measurement — the check has forbidden `'pending'` since the table was created, so no row can ever have carried it. (A shape-only snapshot at 2026-09-16T00:45Z: 707 rows across `received`/`delivered`/`sent`/`pending_review`. Deliberately not pinned as a fixed total in the verification query — this is a live table that gained six rows in the ten minutes between two readings while the migration was written, so an exact count would be stale before it was run, which is the same false-specification failure the migration exists to remove. The query asserts `count(*) where status='pending' = 0` instead.) `drop default` is catalogue-only: no row rewrite, instant at any size. No constraint change (`messages_status_check` keeps its name and all nine values), and no runtime behaviour change. **But `db/types.ts` IS affected, and a first draft of this entry claimed the opposite** — Supabase marks a column optional in the generated `Insert` type when it has a default, so `messages.status` is `status?: string` in `Insert` TODAY *because of* the dead default, and dropping it makes that field REQUIRED on the next `npm run db:types`. Measured, not predicted: hand-patching the type to `status: string` and running `tsc` yields EXACTLY ONE error repo-wide — `lib/agent/schedule-and-send.ts(242,3)`, the return of `buildOutboundInsert`, whose base object omits `status` and relies on `...overrides` (`Partial<MessageInsert>`, every field optional) to supply it. Both callers do supply it at runtime, so it is a type-level gap only. **Applying the migration is safe alone; `npm run db:types` is the step that turns it into a red CI.** **The one-line repair ships in the same PR** — the single deviation from TAC-416's migration-only scope, taken because step 3 of this file's own migration workflow is "Operator runs `npm run db:types`", so the DOCUMENTED next action after applying 046 is the one that reddens CI, and deferring would arm a landmine in a file the follow-up PR never mentions. `buildOutboundInsert`'s `overrides` becomes `Partial<MessageInsert> & Required<Pick<MessageInsert, 'status'>>`, and `db/types.ts:806` is hand-patched to `status: string` per this file's own hand-patch convention. **`Required<Pick<...>>`, not a bare `Pick<...>`: `Pick` PRESERVES optionality**, so a bare Pick is inert until the types flip and a caller could drop `status` meanwhile. Mutation-verified in both schema states — deleting `status: 'sent'` from the auto-send caller fails TS2345 at `schedule-and-send.ts(522,44)` against today's types and against the regenerated ones. Zero runtime change: both callers already pass `status`. **Deliberately dropped rather than corrected**: inbound rows are `received` and drafts are `draft`/`pending_review`, so no single value covers both and picking either would make the wrong one a silent fallback for the other path. After this, an insert omitting `status` fails on NOT NULL instead of on the check — both fail, but the new failure names the actual problem. **Rollback restores a DEAD default** and is only for undoing this migration cleanly. **Ordering doesn't matter** — no deployed read path references a column default, so neither direction opens a window. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`).** The cost being paid here is not a runtime bug: the schema asserted something false and was believed — during TAC-411 the dead default was cited as justification for making `status` optional in a Zod schema, and that reasoning reached a code comment and a CLAUDE.md entry before review caught it. **A schema-wide sweep found this is the only instance** — see the gotcha below.

- `047_ongoing_order_capture.sql` — TAC-325: widens `transactions_source_check` (same drop-and-recreate pattern as migration 034's own change to the identical constraint) to add `guest_reported_ongoing` — a guest's self-reported order AFTER enrollment either already happened or its 7-day window closed. A disjoint `source` value, not a reuse of `guest_reported`, so enrollment's own storage-layer invariant (`idx_transactions_one_guest_reported_per_guest`, migration 034) never sees an ongoing row and a guest can still only ever enroll once. No new index — the same-venue-local-day merge/dedupe is app-level (`lib/agent/extract-reported-order.ts`), since "same calendar day" needs the venue's timezone, which isn't a column on `transactions`. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `transactions`).** Additive per CLAUDE.md's own Ordering rule, but apply in Studio **BEFORE** merging anyway, mirroring migration 034's identical deviation and for the identical reason: the extractor never throws, so a pre-migration CHECK rejection is caught and logged, not crashed — but the guest's report is silently and permanently lost with no retry. No `db/types.ts` change (`source` is a plain `string` there; CHECK values don't surface in generated types).
- `048_instagram_identity_and_message_channel.sql` — TAC-467: the schema an Instagram guest needs, and nothing that writes it (TAC-468 does). Six changes, one transaction. (1) `guests.phone_number` drops NOT NULL; `guests_phone_number_check` and `UNIQUE (venue_id, phone_number)` stay as they are, because a CHECK passes on NULL and NULLs are distinct under a unique constraint. (2) `guests.instagram_scoped_id` (the IGSID), with a non-blank CHECK and **`UNIQUE (venue_id, instagram_scoped_id)` — per venue, not global, deliberately** (the ticket first said global): an IGSID is scoped to one app-and-account pair, so it is not a person identifier. While `venues.instagram_account_id` is globally unique (change 6), an IGSID can only reach the one venue that owns its account, so per venue and global behave the same today. Per venue is chosen because it mirrors `UNIQUE (venue_id, phone_number)` and stays correct if an account is ever allowed to map to more than one venue row. **A first version of this rationale said two venue rows could share one account, which change 6 in the same migration rules out; code review caught it before the migration was applied.** A table constraint rather than a partial index, so a handler can upsert with `onConflict: 'venue_id,instagram_scoped_id'` (PostgREST cannot target a partial index). No format check: samples are 16-digit strings, but Meta documents no format, and a rejected insert on the live webhook path loses the guest's message. (3) `guests_must_have_identity` CHECK: a phone or an IGSID, at least one. (4) `messages.channel text not null default 'text'` with CHECK `in ('text', 'instagram')`. `'text'` is iMessage or SMS through the phone-number provider; not `'sms'` (most are iMessage) and not a vendor name. **The default is a known hazard kept on purpose** — see the gotcha under Common gotchas. (5) `messages.referral_ref` and `messages.referral_source`, nullable, no CHECK: the `ref` and `source` an ig.me link carries, delivered once with the guest's first action and unrecoverable afterwards, stored on the message they arrived with. `type` is not stored (`OPEN_THREAD` is the only value seen, and it follows from a ref being present). (6) `venues.instagram_account_id`, globally unique: maps an inbound event's `entry.id` / `recipient.id` to a venue; without it TAC-468 cannot route. No backfill, no new index beyond the two unique constraints'. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `guests` and `messages`).** It takes every lock up front, `messages` first, under a 5-second `lock_timeout`: altering `guests` first could deadlock with a Sendblue inbound, which holds `messages` and then needs `guests` for its foreign-key check, and the webhook answers 200 on a failed insert, so the guest's text would be lost with no retry. A busy table makes the migration fail cleanly instead; apply outside Le Mil's hours regardless. Order-independent against the deploy (it relaxes one constraint and adds everything else, and no deployed code writes a null phone or reads a new column), **but do not run `npm run db:types` on a `main` without the PR**: regenerated types make the phone nullable and `tsc` fails at the nine sites the PR fixes. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit. The rollback in the file's footer fails once a phoneless guest exists, by design.
- `049_instagram_guest_profile_and_provider_sent_at.sql` — TAC-479: two unrelated changes sharing one review. (1) `messages.provider_sent_at timestamptz`: when the provider says the message was sent, by the provider's clock. The Instagram handler writes it on message, postback and echo rows from the `messaging[]` item's `timestamp` (NOT `entry.time`, 0.4 to 1.1 seconds later in every recorded payload, and far later on a redelivery). It is written on echoes deliberately, because TAC-469 reads it off outbound rows. No default, so Sendblue rows stay NULL; no CHECK, because it is written on the live webhook path; anything that is not a millisecond epoch is parsed to NULL, so a value in seconds never reads as 1970. Nothing that reads `created_at` switched to it. (2) `guests.instagram_username`, `instagram_name`, `instagram_profile_fetched_at` (last SUCCESSFUL fetch) and `instagram_profile_attempted_at` (last attempt, the claim and the retry throttle), with non-blank CHECKs on the two text columns so an absent value is NULL, never `''`. No uniqueness on the handle: handles change, and two rows can briefly hold the same one. `profile_pic` is not stored (its URL expires in days), and follower count and verified status are never requested. No backfill, no index. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages` and `guests`).** Additive, but **apply in Studio BEFORE the PR merges**: Vercel deploys on merge, every Instagram insert then names `provider_sent_at`, and against a missing column that insert fails behind a 200 and the guest's message is lost. Locks `messages` then `guests` up front with a 5-second `lock_timeout` (048's deadlock reasoning). `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit; `npm run db:types` is safe on any branch afterwards, since no code builds a full `guests` or `messages` row literal.
- `050_followup_log_manual_task.sql` — TAC-469 PR B: one nullable `manual_task_recorded_at timestamptz` on `followup_log`, plus a CHECK that it and `message_id` are never both set, plus a partial index on `(venue_id, manual_task_recorded_at desc)` for the read TAC-486 makes. An Instagram follow-up is RECORDED, never sent: the 24-hour reply window is usually shut when one fires and only the guest reopens it, so the engine runs its detectors, Gate 1 and its claim exactly as for SMS and then marks the claim as a task. **The claim is KEPT, which is the point** — the dedup burns as a send would, so the guest is not re-detected every morning for the same visit, and the task counts toward the weekly cap because from the guest's side it is the touch. **A timestamp, not the `manual_task_id` the plan named** (ruled 2026-09-19): there is no task table for an id to reference, `followup_log.id` is already the handle TAC-486 joins on, and a `_id` column pointing at nothing is a name promising a foreign key it does not have. Its one real job is telling a recorded task from an ORPHANED claim, since both leave `message_id` null — so the orphan-claim audit query becomes `message_id is null and manual_task_recorded_at is null`. NO BACKFILL and nullable rather than defaulted: a default would claim every historical SMS send was a task. Additive, but the deployed engine WRITES the column on its next hourly tick, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging**, the call migration 029 made on this table — the engine never throws into the cron, so a missing column surfaces as a claim that can never be finalised, burning the dedup with nothing recorded. Not on the high-stakes table list. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit.

- `051_venue_guest_activity.sql` — TAC-476: a new RPC `venue_guest_activity(p_venue_id uuid)` returning `(guest_id, last_inbound_at, last_outbound_at, last_interaction_at)` as `max(created_at)` grouped by guest and direction, plus a `comment on column` on each of the three `guests` columns it replaces. **`guests.last_inbound_at` and `last_interaction_at` were written once at guest creation and never updated, and `last_outbound_at` has never been written by anything** — so all three recorded FIRST CONTACT, and on 35 of 36 rows they hold the same value as `first_contacted_at` to the millisecond, because one insert sets them all from the same `nowIso`. Their two readers were the follow-up engine's recent-conversation gate and the Command Center conversations dropdown. **The gate failed OPEN three times in production** (dispatching 1.7, 4.5 and 6.4 hours after the guest's real previous inbound), and for the 20 of 35 scannable guests whose column is NULL it never ran at all — `if (guest.lastInboundAt !== null)` short-circuits, and one of those guests has 122 inbound messages. **Deriving was chosen over keeping the columns current (ruled 2026-09-20), and the argument generalises**: keeping them current needs six write sites, every one on a live send or receive path, on handlers that log-and-return-200 on failure — so a silently failed UPDATE would reintroduce this exact defect invisibly, which is the failure being fixed. A fix that can fail the same way the original did is not a fix. Deriving also needs no backfill (correct for every existing row including the NULLs on the day it ships), cannot drift, and **drops the tier**: it never opens the Sendblue webhook handler or the Instagram handler, so a hard-stop ticket became plan-gate. Precedent: TAC-469's Instagram window gate, `app/api/cron/webhook-silence`'s own last-inbound derivation, and `count_outbound_responses` (migration 032). **The function counts EVERY message row** — no `body <> ''`, no status filter, no `review_state` filter — deliberately NOT importing the reached-guest condition (migrations 043/044), which exists so operator-facing reads show only what the guest received; tying a suppression rule and a dropdown sort to it would couple them to a delivery-status list maintained for a different purpose. It reads `created_at`, never `provider_sent_at`: Instagram rows carry Meta's clock and Sendblue rows never do, so ordering on it would sort the two channels on different clocks. **HIGH-STAKES by the 043/044 precedent (it reads `messages`)** — additive, but deployed code calls it, so apply in Studio BEFORE merging. `create or replace` is correct for a first version; a later RETURN-TYPE change must DROP and CREATE in one transaction (migration 039's gotcha). `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit — **RPCs DO surface under `Functions`**, contrary to what migration 023's entry says. The three columns stay for now because removing them means editing the Sendblue webhook handler; TAC-503 removes them and the `comment on column` is the interim mitigation.
- `052_messages_pending_cancellation.sql` — TAC-513: one nullable `jsonb` on `messages`, `pending_cancellation`, holding the commitment a queued draft WITHDRAWS, as `{"commitmentId": <uuid>}`. On 2026-09-21 at Le Mil's the agent wrote "the comp for the blossom tonic is cancelled" and nothing cancelled it: comp `GWPZ` stayed `open` while the guest believed it was gone, because no field existed that could carry a cancellation, so the only way to say that sentence was to say it falsely. Shaped like `pending_commitment` (027) and `rendered_intentions` (045): a jsonb intent carrier on the draft row, camelCase inside the payload, acted on only at dispatch. **A SECOND COLUMN rather than a member of `pending_commitment`, for two reasons.** Migration 041's two partial unique index predicates read `pending_commitment->>'type'` to pick the pending slot and `PendingCommitmentSchema.safeParse` gates whether `createCommitmentFromPending` runs at all, so a `type: 'cancellation'` member would have to be taught to both — and a slot predicate on a live table is not a thing to teach new vocabulary. And a reply can legitimately do both ("that comp's off, but come back for a pastry"); one column cannot express that, two can, and the draft then routes to the obligation slot on the strength of the offer, which is correct. **Referenced by ID, never by code** (ruled with the plan): `generateCommitmentCode` draws 4 chars from a 31-char alphabet with no uniqueness constraint anywhere, so two open comps for one guest can collide, and `recommendation` rows carry `code = NULL` by construction so a code-keyed reference cannot address them at all. The id is already rendered in `## Active commitments` and already copied verbatim by the model into `arrivalCapture.referencesCommitmentId`; TAC-302 is the recorded failure of the alternative, where the id was absent, the model reached for the 4-char code and every arrival capture no-op'd. **NO BACKFILL, NO INDEX** (the only read is by primary key, inside `dispatchOperatorOutbound`). NULL means "cancels nothing, or predates this" and both read the same way. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`)** — additive, but deployed code SELECTs it, so apply in Studio BEFORE merging, the call 025/026/027/034/035/036/038/039/045 all made. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit until `npm run db:types` runs post-apply. Rollback (`alter table messages drop column pending_cancellation`) is safe at any time: nothing else reads the column, and dropping it loses only the carrier on drafts still sitting in the queue.

- `053_ungrounded_claims_comment.sql` — TAC-424: **catalogue only**, a single `comment on column messages.ungrounded_claims`. No column, no constraint, no index, no row rewrite, no `db/types.ts` change (comments do not surface in generated types). Migration 039's comment ended "a TRANSIENT verifier fault fails open and records as empty, not NULL", which TAC-424 made false: the transient case is its own `degraded` state now, maps to NULL, and holds the draft. **The comment matters more than most here** — this column exists so a question can be asked in SQL, and the comment is what someone reads first when they open it in Studio to ask it, so leaving it would have the artefact people check against assert the exact belief the ticket removed (migration 046's lesson, restated). The replacement names all five outcomes and says which of the three stored values each takes, points at `review_triggers` for telling the two no-verdict causes apart, and carries the HISTORY sentence that matters for reading old rows: before TAC-424, EMPTY could mean a transient fault that sent, so pre-ticket rows cannot be trusted to mean "checked and clean" (ruling 3 A left them as they are). **TAC-424's ruling 1 C said no migration on `messages`**, which is why the code shipped without one; this file is the operator's own call (2026-09-21) that a catalogue-only statement falls outside that. **Numbered 053, not 052** — TAC-513 holds 052. **Ordering does not matter**: nothing in this repo reads a column comment, so apply before or after merge.
- `054_conversation_cards_per_reply.sql` — TAC-397: the conversation slot becomes one card PER INBOUND, plus the two columns that keep what a correction replaced. Three changes, one transaction, because old code must never see the new index without the new columns and RPC. (1) `messages.replaced_draft_body` / `replaced_draft_at`, nullable, no default, no backfill, written together or not at all by `tryRegenUpdate` and cleared on every regen that is NOT a correction — a card since overwritten by the decline or the crash card must not still show text some earlier correction displaced. (2) migration 041's `idx_messages_one_pending_conversation_per_guest` is replaced by `idx_messages_one_pending_conversation_per_guest_reply`, keyed on `(venue_id, guest_id, coalesce(reply_to_message_id, '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000'::uuid))` with 041's predicate unchanged. **The `coalesce` is load-bearing and its omission is the mistake to avoid**: NULLs are distinct in a unique index, so a bare column would give proactive conversation cards (manual followups, the decline, the crash card, engine followups) NO uniqueness at all — protection 041 provides today — and two concurrent manual followups would both INSERT. Same trick 041's own predicate uses on `pending_commitment->>'type'`, for the same reason. **Why an index over a cap:** a partial unique index cannot express "at most N", which needs a trigger; `reply_to_message_id` is the right key because `buildOutboundInsert` and `tryRegenUpdate` both set it to the current inbound's id, so each DISTINCT inbound owns at most one conversation card while a correction's regen moves the column onto the correcting message and keeps the index satisfied by construction. **It cannot fail to build**: 041 guarantees at most one conversation row per `(venue_id, guest_id)` and the new key is strictly finer, so no backfill and no pre-clean — which is why the new index is created BEFORE 041's is dropped, in one transaction, leaving the table never unguarded. Not `CONCURRENTLY` (cannot run in a transaction). The obligation index is UNTOUCHED. (3) `list_operator_queue` DROP+CREATE restating 044's body with the two new return columns — a new return column is a signature change, so `create or replace` is refused (039's rule). **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`).** Apply in Studio BEFORE merge, outside Le Mil's hours; the window is materially safer than 041's own, because the new index is strictly LOOSER for old code (it permits rows 041 forbade and forbids nothing 041 allowed), so no old-code write that succeeded before can start failing. **New code against 041, however, fails on every second conversation card**: the INSERT hits 041's per-guest index, recovery finds no card for this inbound, decides `insert` again and exhausts `RACE_RECOVERY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` into a red alert — pinned as a deploy-window test in `two-pending-slots.test.ts` beside the existing 020 one. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit; **RPC return columns surface under `Functions`** and are typed non-null there, which is why `normalizeReplacedDraft` casts and re-checks. One edge recorded rather than solved: `reply_to_message_id` is `on delete set null`, so deleting an inbound that two pending drafts reference would collapse both onto the sentinel and fail that DELETE on the unique index.

- `055_inbound_turn_outcomes.sql` — TAC-523: one row per inbound turn, saying what came of it. **A COMPLETE LEDGER, not a failure log** (ruled 2026-09-23): successes are recorded too, because a failure count without a denominator answers "what went wrong" but not "how often does anything go wrong", and reconstructing the denominator by joining back to `messages` is exactly the reconstruction this table exists to stop. **Why it exists:** both webhooks call `waitUntil(runInboundAgent(id))` and DISCARD the returned `AgentResult`, and eighteen distinct paths can end a turn with no outbound row — none of which wrote anything queryable, so from the database a swallowed reply was indistinguishable from a message nobody answered. The 2026-09-20 incident was diagnosable only because Vercel still held the runtime logs; a day later it would not have been. **What counts as a turn:** a guest action that could have warranted a reply. An Instagram echo, a read receipt and a redelivery of an already-saved event are deliberately NOT recorded — each is still a DECISION in code (`resolveAgentHandoff` returns `not_a_turn` and `tsc` refuses a new outcome shape until it picks one), never an omission. `skipped_duplicate` IS recorded, so a strict turn count is `where outcome <> 'skipped_duplicate'`. **All three identity columns are nullable and that is the design**: a Sendblue bail at "venue not found" has no venue, no guest and no message, and a record requiring them could not describe the case it exists for. `outbound_message_id` is `on delete set null`, NOT cascade — `lib/operator/dispatch-instagram-outbound.ts`'s echo-fold is the one place in this repo that DELETEs a `messages` row, and cascading would take the ledger entry with it. **No unique constraint, deliberately**: Meta redelivers, a redelivery is a real second event, and deduping would hide the retry storms this makes visible. **Why a new table** rather than `audit_log` (zero readers and zero writers since migration 001 — its free-text `action` would put the reason vocabulary in untyped jsonb, and it has no guest or message column), a column on `messages` (structurally cannot record the Sendblue bails, which happen BEFORE the row exists), or `engagement_events` (feeds `ENGAGEMENT_EVENT_WEIGHTS`; a reply that did not happen is not a guest action — the TAC-324 precedent). The `reason` CHECK already carries the nine Sendblue bail reasons, which nothing writes yet, so **PR 2 is code-only**. **Volume, measured 2026-09-23** so a future reader can re-judge rather than re-derive: Le Mil's 79 inbound in 7 days and 138 in 30 (~11/day, mostly test traffic), Mock Sextant 25 in 30 days, Central Perk none; at ten venues with real traffic, an order of magnitude more per venue is roughly 100-1,000 rows/day fleet-wide. **No pruning strategy is designed and none is needed at that rate.** Additive, a new table only, but deployed code INSERTs into it on the very next inbound after deploy, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging** — the call 026 / 029 / 035 all made. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit.

- `056_operator_instagram_fields.sql` — TAC-473: what the operator app needs to tell an Instagram guest from a text guest, see how long is left to reply, and record a card answered from outside. Five changes, one transaction. (1) `messages.resolved_by_message_id` (nullable, self-FK `on delete set null`): which Instagram echo answered this pending card. **Deliberately NULL when an operator asserted the send by hand** through the new endpoint — an operator saying they sent something is a weaker record than an echo proving it, and the two must stay tellable apart in SQL. The cascade should never fire (the one path that deletes a `messages` row, `stampInstagramOperatorSend`'s echo-fold, only ever touches OUR OWN sends, which can never be the echo that resolved a card); it is there so that if it ever does, the resolution survives with a weaker record rather than the delete failing. (2) `messages.window_warning_pushed_at` (nullable): the one-hour push's idempotency marker. **Durable state, not a log** — the processor ticks every minute against an hour-long window, so without it one card pushes sixty times, which is migration 038's escalation lesson restated. (3) `messages_review_state_check` gains `'resolved_externally'`, a sixth value. A card answered from the Instagram app was not approved, edited, skipped or auto-sent, and reusing `'skipped'` would record an operator verdict nobody gave while corrupting the skip rate. **`messages_previous_review_state_check` is deliberately NOT widened**: nothing writes the value there, and `/undo` gates on `last_operator_action_at` plus an operator match so it cannot reach such a row — a value permitted in a column nothing writes is a claim the schema cannot back. (4) `list_operator_queue` and (5) `list_operator_conversations`, both **DROP + CREATE** restating 054's and 043's bodies verbatim with only additions, because adding a return column is a return-type change Postgres refuses to replace (039's rule; 043 was a `create or replace` only because it changed the body alone). **The queue returns the DRAFT ROW's `channel`, not one re-derived from the guest** — `dispatchOperatorOutbound` routes on the card's channel, so the column is exactly "what approving this card will do", and a re-derivation could disagree with the routing. **The conversations function returns `resolveConversationChannel`'s INPUTS and lets TS resolve**, rather than restating that rule in SQL where two copies would agree until one changed; its Instagram identifier is a BOOLEAN, not the scoped ID, since the resolver needs only presence and an IGSID in a projection is one typo from the wire. Both window anchors **mirror `loadLastGuestActionAt` filter for filter** — that function is what the send gate consults, so a different answer here would show the operator a deadline the server would not honour — and **the 24 hours is NOT written in SQL**: TS adds `INSTAGRAM_WINDOW_MS`, so the constant has one definition and needs no binding test. **HIGH-STAKES (touches `messages`).** Additive, but deployed code SELECTs the new RPC columns, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging** — merging first breaks `GET /api/operator/queue` and `GET /api/operator/conversations` outright. `lock_timeout = '5s'` up front per 048/049. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit. The rollback restores both function bodies FIRST (a SQL function's body is a string and carries no column dependencies, so dropping a column it selects succeeds and leaves every operator read failing at call time), and its CHECK restore ABORTS if any row already carries the new value, which is correct: those are cards a human was told were handled, and there is no honest value to rewrite them to.
- `057_inbound_turn_coalescing.sql` — TAC-526: `inbound_turn_claims`, keyed `primary key (venue_id, guest_id)`, so a guest's burst produces one reply instead of one per message. **The defect:** both webhooks call `waitUntil(runInboundAgent(id))` once per inbound row, so two messages seconds apart start two runs in two serverless invocations that share no memory; observed live at Le Mil's 2026-09-23, 7 seconds between the guest's messages, 5 between the replies, and the guest asked their name twice. **The ticket's premise was half wrong and the half that is wrong decides the design:** both runs could see the other's MESSAGE (`build-runtime-context.ts` excludes only `currentMessage.id`), neither could see the other's REPLY because it did not exist yet — so the fix is "only one run may produce a reply", which is why this is a claim table and **no prompt file is touched and `PROMPT_VERSION` is not bumped**. **Why a table and not a column on `messages`:** verified before choosing — `status` is CHECK-constrained to nine values with no claim state (001), `updated_at` is trigger-maintained so it cannot be a CAS witness, and every column already used as a claim (`pending_until`, `review_state`, `generated_by`) is outbound-only; a claim column means a migration against `messages`, so **this ticket ships no migration against `messages` at all**, a deliberate property rather than an accident of scope. **The primary key IS the mechanism**: the store does a plain INSERT with **no `ON CONFLICT`**, so a race surfaces as 23505 and exactly one run wins — `claimFollowupLogRows` (`followups/log.ts`) is the same idiom against the same class of race, and an upsert that swallowed the conflict would hand both runs a success. One Instagram delivery can carry several guest messages inserted in the same millisecond (`entry[] × messaging[]`), so `order by created_at desc` is not a total order on its own; that is the concrete reason the claim is load-bearing rather than ceremony, and why `pickNewer` compares on the `(created_at, id)` PAIR. **`expires_at` is a BACKSTOP, not the mechanism** — the normal path releases explicitly in a `finally`; the lease covers only a function killed without running any code (OOM, wall-clock), and takeover of an expired claim is CAS-gated on the holder's `agent_run_id` still being the one just read (`refresh-profile.ts`'s `claimed_elsewhere` shape) so two runs finding one expired claim cannot both take it. A claim is live while `now < expires_at`, so the exact expiry instant counts as expired; both sides are pinned by test because the first test written for it asserted the opposite and neither reading had been decided. **One row, not a history** — rows are deleted on release, so the table is bounded by the guests in conversation at one instant. No index beyond the primary key: every read is by the full key. **Second half:** drops and recreates `inbound_turn_outcomes_reason_check` to add `coalesced_into_turn` (widening a CHECK has no `ALTER CONSTRAINT`, so it is the drop-and-recreate pattern 011/012/016/034/047 use), **so 057 now owns the `reason` constraint and 055 still owns `outcome`/`layer`/`channel`** — `lib/schemas/inbound-turn-outcome.test.ts` reads whichever migration owns each, and reading 055 for `reason` would bind the constants to a constraint the database no longer has. **Verify `inbound_turn_outcomes_reason_check` against `pg_constraint` before applying**: the name is Postgres's own for 055's inline CHECK, and a name assumed rather than checked is how a drop removes the wrong constraint. Additive, but deployed code writes both the table and the new reason on the next coalesced turn, so **apply in Studio BEFORE merging** — the call 026/029/035/050/055 all made. **Rollback caveat that is not cosmetic:** narrowing the CHECK back ABORTS if any row already carries `coalesced_into_turn`, so the rollback runs before, or together with, deleting those rows; the file's footer carries both statements. `db/types.ts` hand-patched in the same commit. No sweep cron for claims orphaned by a killed function: the lease bounds them, takeover is CAS-gated, and a stale row is overwritten by that guest's next turn rather than accumulating.

RLS policies will be added in a future migration before any external user gets DB access (THE-110).
