Fix reuses `firstTouchAfterQrScan` (the same flag driving R1's carve-out — no second definition of first touch) to LEAD `formatOpenIntentions`'s output with an opener paragraph on a guest's true first message, in the model's own words every time. **The paragraph is split, not unconditional** — code review on the first draft caught that `firstTouchAfterQrScan` is content-blind (it fires on ANY qr_scan guest's true first message, not just a bare greeting), so an unconditional "ask if it's their first time" would fight a real first question ("are you open right now?") for the turn. Saying hello and identifying yourself never conflicts with answering a question, so that half stays unconditional; the first-time question explicitly defers to whatever the guest's own message actually asks — answered if they asked something, asked if they didn't. Explicitly carries the never-texted-vs-never-visited distinction (`created_via: 'qr_scan'` means never-texted, not never-visited) so the question reads as genuinely open rather than hollow against a `Guest relationship: new` line that only reflects absence of signals, not absence of history. Leads rather than appends: appending directly after "Never steer back to them" made "them" ambiguous and framed the opener as an exception to a prohibition rather than this turn's actual job. **Tradeoff, not fixed here:** the opener lives behind the same `lines.length === 0` guard as the rest of the block, so a `guest_intention_prompts` read failure (fails CLOSED per above) empties `openIntentions` and silently removes the opener along with it — on exactly the turn this ticket exists to fix. Accepted for pilot scale. **Compounds TAC-328** (filed separately, out of scope here): the intentions block's render gate doesn't exclude `opt_out`, and this ticket adds a more directive paragraph to that same ungated block — raises TAC-328's real-world severity without fixing it. **TAC-330 (v1.35.0) fixes the turn TAC-329's own UAT list named as the next beat: reply "first time!" to the opener, and instead of following up on the order, Sana recommended a drink.** Two independent causes. First, the non-steering paragraph is symmetric — it had no way to distinguish the guest raising their own topic from the guest answering something Sana herself just asked, so the turn-two reply drew the same restraint as an unprompted pivot. `formatOpenIntentions` appends a bounded exception (the original four sentences stay byte-identical): when Sana's own last message asked the guest something about themselves (new vs. regular) and the reply answers it, following up is not a pivot. Deliberately narrower than "Sana's last message was any question" — that condition would have licensed a pivot after almost any exchange (plan-review's own counter-example: a parking Q&A closing with "you heading in soon?" would have qualified), which is close to the exact pivot the paragraph exists to prevent; residual risk accepted rather than solved is that the model actually generalizes from the worked exemplar ("new or a regular"), not a crisp category boundary — see the comment above `formatOpenIntentions` in `serializers.ts`. Second, the recommendation itself came from `venue_configs.venue_info` — `menu.notes` and `menu.highlights` phrased the owner's first-timer pick as an imperative addressed to the persona ("don't over-program the first visit, let them meet the Maiden Voyage") rather than an attributed fact, and an imperative in the prompt beats a goal that invites judgement. Rewritten to indicative, attributed form at Mock Sextant (a live data UPDATE, not a migration — `venue_info`'s shape is unchanged); three more instances of the identical mood problem found auditing the rest of the column (`hours.notes`, two `menu.items[].description` fields) fixed the same conservative way, preserving the informational content rather than deleting it. The extractor that produces this imperative mood at every new venue onboarded is out of scope here — TAC-331 owns it. **TAC-330's own live UAT surfaced a second, independent cause of the same turn failing (case 2): `acknowledgment` category instructions silently vetoing the block above whenever a terse reply misclassified into that category.** Fixed at v1.36.0 — see "Category instruction layer carries NO pursuit authority (TAC-327)" above for the fix itself. Not live-UAT-reverified as of v1.36.0, sequenced behind TAC-332 (a separate, unrelated intention-recording defect). **TAC-423 (v1.52.0, then rewritten at v1.60.0) made the opener state the situation, ask what the guest just got, and prescribe nothing else.** The QR's placement is assumed to be the pickup counter (ruled 2026-09-18; not venue-configurable, since a placement field would carry exactly one value while there is one venue). v1.52.0 changed the opener's scripted question from "ask whether it's their first time" to "ask what they got", which stopped it racing `understand_order` (the top-priority intention, arming on this exact turn since TAC-436's `visit_confirmed`) by pointing both at the same target. **That fix failed its device check and the ticket was reopened**: the reply read "Hey, welcome! You're texting Himanshu directly. What did you end up getting?" — correct against the written gate, wrong as hospitality. v1.60.0 keeps a scripted question but reduces it to one present-tense sentence, `Ask what they just got.`, and **that question is SCAFFOLDING rather than the intended design.** The intended design is the opener stating facts while the intention lines beneath carry the ask, `understand_order` being first among them on this turn with a line that says exactly what that sentence says. **It was built that way and measured, and the intention line could not carry it** (`scripts/measurement/first-touch-question.ts`, 20 generations per arm on Le Mil's live config, 2026-09-22): with the opener silent the reply still asked SOMETHING 20/20, but asked about the ORDER only **11/20, against 20/20** with the opener asking. The nine misses are worse than the rate. **Five asked how it was**, which is `did_they_like_it` — an intention not even open on that turn, since it arms on a recorded order and there is none — and an answer naming no item captures nothing and gives `reportsTodaysScanVisit` nothing to fire on. **Four reverted to asking whether it was the guest's first time**, the behaviour this ticket was filed to delete, with nothing in the prompt asking for it; v1.52.0 had only suppressed it by scripting over the top. An opener that reintroduces the original bug half the time is not an improvement on a scripted one (ruled 2026-09-22). **The question comes out when TAC-519 establishes why intentions are so rarely raised and fixes it**, and that harness is what should decide it. At 55% the intention line cannot carry the ask alone. **TAC-519 settled it and the answer is that the question STAYS.** That ticket found the real cause of the low raise rate (the block rendered 3rd of the user prompt rather than last) and fixed it; with the fix, the intention line carries the order ask on **28 of 40 first-touch generations, against the scripted question's 40 of 40**, and one generation still reverted to asking whether it was the guest's first time. **The floor was RE-MEASURED at 26/40 (65%) rather than inherited**, because TAC-423's own run log was not recoverable: `createRunLog` writes to `measurement-runs/` relative to cwd, no `tac423-first-touch-question*.jsonl` exists anywhere, and that worktree is gone. So 11/20 (55%) is not reproducible and 65% is the number to quote. The arm itself is now DERIVED from the live constant (the shipped opener minus its final sentence) and throws on drift, rather than transcribed, so it cannot silently measure a different opener: that guard fired on its first real use, when TAC-423 merged mid-session and a stale worktree still held v1.52.0's text. **The shipped wording was then confirmed on the same harness at 20/20 on both scenarios**, matching v1.52.0, so the scripted question restores what the silent opener lost. **Read that confirmation run's history before trusting any future one**: it first reported 71%, entirely because the detector matched exact phrases and the shipped opener's own word `just` made the model write "what did you just grab?". That was the SECOND asymmetric detector gap in one ticket (contractions were the first), and both pointed the same way, against whichever arm was not echoing a script. The matcher is patterns with an adverb slot now. Re-scoring the first run with it leaves 55% unchanged, which is what shows the ruling rests on a real difference rather than on either gap. Three further changes, each ruled 2026-09-22:
  - **The thank-you is gone from the prescription.** Le Mil's caps replies at "one-liners or two sentences at most" and R20 makes `## Length` the only authority on length, so prescribing a hello, an introduction, a thank-you and a question into a two-sentence budget meant the model dropped one, and it dropped the warmth. The reply is a hello and one question by design. **Warmth is voice, not a clause** — do not re-add it here.
  - **The identity clause is conditional and states that it outranks the persona.** It fires only when the guest's own message names no person, and says so explicitly, because `speakerFramingProse`'s `owner` branch renders "Do not name yourself unless the guest asks" while this paragraph renders later in the user prompt and was already overriding it silently. Le Mil's prefill (`qrEnrollmentMessage`, now "Hi Le Mil's!") names the venue and not a person, so every ordinary scan takes the introduce branch.
  - **Present tense, and it is load-bearing.** "have just ordered and collected it" replaces "have already ordered and have it in hand ... what it **was**". The recency sits on the ORDER, never on the guest's whereabouts, so R1's "without assuming they're still on-site" carve-out is untouched — that carve-out exists because the agent once told a guest who had left that the password was on the board.
  **Both CLAUSES that followed the old question are gone** — a separate thing from the question itself, which is back — because the restraint paragraph rendered directly beneath says both ("take the one listed first, and only that one"; "Asking never changes what the reply is about ... the question goes at the end, in one short line, or not at all"). The second was also the deadlock sentence TAC-436 deleted from that paragraph, surviving in the opener in different words and so invisible to the canary guarding it — **the opener now carries a canary on its own wording too.** Consequence, ruled rather than inherited: a guest who scans AND asks something gets their answer plus one short question, where the opener used to hold the question back. **The rationale for that one did NOT survive measurement, and is recorded rather than quietly kept:** the deferral clause was expected to suppress the ask on exactly that turn shape, and the old opener asked 20/20 there anyway, so on this turn the clause was inert. TAC-436's own measurement was of the restraint paragraph on ordinary turns, a different population, and stands. The clause stays out on the ruling, not on this evidence. **The Instagram variant is now ONE phrase swap, down from two** ("who they've reached" is true on both channels, so the texting/messaging row is gone); adding a second back is a deliberate scope change the guard in `serializers.test.ts` fails until someone makes it.
  **A guest who answers is captured through TAC-323's enrolment path** (gates 2 and 3 both hold on a first or second message), and everything after through TAC-325's ongoing path — both confirmed live at Le Mil's.
  **TAC-423 also taught the extractor that a scan-day report is a receipt** (`reportsTodaysScanVisit`, `lib/agent/extract-reported-order.ts`), and the reason is the whole point of re-tensing the opener: the extractor's own prompt reads a report carrying **no timing cue at all** as one about today, dates it to venue-local noon and records it `approximate`, and an approximate visit blocks `detectPostVisitReason` outright. "the blossom tonic" is exactly the answer the opener's question gets, so the common case was silently losing the post-visit followup ladder — measured at Le Mil's, one of five scanned guests carried a `pinned` visit. Three conditions, all required: the guest was created by a scan, they were created TODAY in venue-local terms, and the report itself resolved to TODAY. **Wider than "no timing cue", deliberately**: the model returns `specific_past_day` for a bare item name AND for "earlier today"/"this morning", and both resolve to today, so both are promoted; the ladder is day-granular, so pinning a 9am drink to a 10am message is not an error it can see. **Precision is resolved by `resolvePresentPrecision`, never asserted** — a scan-day report arriving while the venue reads CLOSED stays approximate, exactly as "just grabbed a cortado" at that hour would, so `pinned` has one definition rather than two. **Nothing changes for any other turn**, which `extract-reported-order.test.ts` pins from both sides (a scan-day no-cue report becomes pinned at the message time; an ordinary guest's identical report stays loose at venue-local noon) plus three boundaries: scanned on an earlier day, a report about another day, and the closed-venue case. **`EXTRACT_REPORTED_ORDER_PROMPT_VERSION` is deliberately NOT bumped** — the extractor's prompt is untouched; this is caller-side resolution.
  **Recording on the opener turn is on** (ruled; see the TAC-332 reversal note under *Intentions, redefined*).

- **Intentions, redefined (TAC-380, v1.49.0).** Supersedes the specifics of the TAC-324 bullet above; its render-gate history (TAC-328/329/330/332) still holds.
  - **Seven intentions**, defined in `lib/agent/intentions/definitions.ts` as a `satisfies Record<IntentionKey, IntentionDefinition>` map — TAC-324 shipped a plain array, which is not exhaustiveness-checked (the `TERMINAL_STATUSES` trap) — and sorted by `priority`: `understand_order` (10, renamed from `learn_first_order`), `got_the_recommendation` (20), `did_they_like_it` (30), `learn_name` (40), `are_they_local` (50), `their_rhythm` (60), `why_theyre_here` (70). **Event-armed intentions rank right after `understand_order` because they perish** (ruling 3): "did you get the Pink Panther?" is worthless in a fortnight. `invite_contact_save` is retired (a guest saving a contact is unobservable, so it was a permanent open loop). Cut before building: capture-only intentions (volunteered information already lands in `contextUpdate`) and `they_said_theyd_come` (its closing move is an outbound, which makes it a followup).
  - **Closure is prompted-once for all seven.** Closing on the guest's actual answer is TAC-385. `isSatisfied` is a second closure where a proxy exists: `understand_order` ← any transaction, `learn_name` ← `guests.first_name`, `are_they_local` ← context `home_base`. The rest have none.
  - **Arming** (`armsOn`): `qr_scan_enrollment` for `understand_order` (the scan confirms a visit, which is what keeps asking about an order R1-safe), `open_recommendation` (the NEWEST open recommendation still inside its window — ruling 1; arming off the first one ever blocked any guest with an old recommendation for good, because recommendations never leave `open`), `recorded_order` for `did_they_like_it` (the NEWEST recorded order, for the same reason, read from the PARSED visit history the context build already loads newest first, which is what `## Visit history` renders, so the model can see the order it is asked about; it replaced a dedicated earliest-transaction query, so the reply path runs one query fewer), and `first_contact` for everyone. **While the newest recommendation or order is still inside its conversation, the intention that asks about it neither arms nor renders**, even off an older event and even as an already-open row: the rendered line doesn't say which event it means and `## Active commitments` lists every open recommendation, so arming off an older one let the model ask about the one it had just suggested. An earlier version fell back to the older event; code review caught it. If the open recommendations can't be read that turn, `got_the_recommendation` is held outright: that read fails closed, as the read at `build-runtime-context.ts:203` does, where an empty list would silently lift the hold. Also caught in review. The TAC-324 `qr_scan`-only origin gate is gone (ruling 6); it was an artifact of these being first-touch intentions, and it excluded the guest this ticket came from.
  - **Gate** (`conversational`): `recognition.signals.responseRate >= intention_rules.response_rate_floor` AND lifetime `repliedMessageCount >= min_replies` (defaults 3/3/3/5/8/11 in priority order, overridable per key). **One ratio floor, staggered on the RAW reply count**, because `normalizeResponseRate` reads 0 until three responses have been sent and ~100 for an engaged guest after that — tiers on the ratio all open on the same turn. `repliedMessageCount` is threaded out of `computeRelationshipStrength` for exactly this. `understand_order` is ungated: asking what someone got needs no permission. Every threshold is a PLACEHOLDER.
  - **State rows** (migration 040). Eligibility is recorded (`prompted_at` null, `eligible_at` set) on the first inbound turn an intention arms and passes its gate, by `recordIntentionEligibility`, fired via `waitUntil` after classification — **never on an `opt_out` turn or a crisis-safety turn**, because the row starts an expiry window and neither turn should record intent to pursue the guest. Skipping loses nothing: eligibility re-derives from live facts on the next inbound. **Expiry runs from `eligible_at`, not guest creation** (ruling 5): from creation, one-per-turn raising leaves the lower-priority intentions expiring unraised, which makes the priority list decorative. First-contact intentions anchor to the turn their gate was first seen open; event-armed ones anchor to the moment their event became part of a DIFFERENT conversation — once it is older than `followup_rules.recent_conversation_hours` (ruling 2: the same number followups and the brake use, no second one) — so "did you try it?" is never asked in the exchange where it was suggested, the whole window stays askable at any configured conversation length (anchored at the event, a 72-hour setting would leave nothing), and they still perish on schedule however late the gate opened. Windows: `understand_order` 3 days, event-armed 3, first-contact 14. **Eligibility is sticky for first-contact intentions** — an existing row decides and the gate is never re-checked; disengagement is the brake's job. Event-armed intentions re-arm instead (next bullet).
  - **Re-arming** (acceptance criteria corrected 2026-09-14). First-contact intentions never re-arm: re-asking is nagging. `got_the_recommendation` and `did_they_like_it` re-arm on a strictly newer recommendation or order (`rearmsOnNewerEvent`, an exhaustive switch in `definitions.ts`), whether the existing row was prompted, ran out unraised, or is still open. Without it, one row per guest per intention meant a guest whose window ran out was never asked about any later event, which is ruling 1's trap one level down. **"Strictly newer" means the event happened after the row's stored `eligible_at`**, i.e. after the earlier event had already become askable. That is ruling 2's one definition of a different visit (a second recommendation from the same conversation is the same thing to ask about), and comparing against the STORED anchor, never the old event recomputed through today's window, means lengthening `recent_conversation_hours` can't make an event look newer than itself. A re-arm is a fresh arming (gate, satisfaction and expiry are checked again) and rides the eligibility write as `rearm: true`. **It moves `eligible_at` and nothing else**: the row keeps its last prompt, the brake still counts it, and the intention reads as open again because that prompt predates the new anchor (`isReopened`, event-armed keys only). **A re-arm waits while the intention's own last prompt went unanswered**, by the brake's own rule, and lifts once that prompt ages out of the visible history. The first version cleared the prompt instead, and code review showed that erased the evidence the brake runs on: a guest who ignored every question but kept ordering was asked after every order, because a single re-arming intention's row only holds one prompt and can never build a streak of two. How the re-arm write and the prompt stamp stay safe in either order is under Common gotchas.
  - **The brake.** When the last `unanswered_streak` (2) prompts — grouped by `message_id`, excluding `prompt_source = 'pessimistic'` — each saw no inbound within `followup_rules.recent_conversation_hours`, nothing renders. **The ticket's first definition ("saw no subsequent inbound") was unreachable**: prompts only record on replies to inbounds, so every earlier prompt is followed by the inbound the next one answered, and the brake would read correctly and never fire — the `comp_regex_backstop` shape again. The window REUSES the followup setting (ruling 1: one definition of "the same conversation"); at the 48h default it rarely fires, which is the intended direction, since a prompt closes on being asked anyway. **Prompts older than the visible inbound history are left out, never counted as unanswered** — see Common gotchas.
  - **Rendering.** Every open line renders, in priority order, plus one sentence: "take the one listed first" (ruling 4). **The block renders LAST of the user prompt's content blocks, immediately before the emoji directive (TAC-519, v1.61.0), and that position is measured rather than chosen.** TAC-324 put it 3rd, beside who-the-guest-is rather than what-was-recently-said; from there three blocks rendered after it on an ordinary turn (`## Visit history`, `## Active commitments`, `## Recent conversation`) and intentions were raised on **4 of the 39 real Le Mil's turns that rendered them in 14 days**, with `learn_name` armed for all 7 guests and asked 0 times ever. Replaying those same 39 turns with only the move applied and everything else byte-for-byte equal took it to **13/35, 11% to 37%**, `learn_name` raised 4 times. Most-proximate-wins, the class of TAC-314/329/330/338/362. **A rewrite of the restraint paragraph was measured in the same run and DROPPED**: inverting its default from "ask when an opening appears" to "ask unless one of these stops you" was worse on both populations and breached the two-questions-in-one-reply ceiling ("Did you just come by today? What did you grab?"), which is the interrogation failure the block exists to prevent. The position was the defect, not the wording, and on theory alone the wrong one would have shipped. **Do not move this block without re-running TAC-519's harness** (`scripts/measurement/first-touch-question.ts --mode ordinary`, the only mode the position is measurable in), and note the emoji directive keeps its own last-block position, separately measured (TAC-362): the full-block-order test in `serializers.test.ts` is the only thing that catches a move past it. **`renderableIntentions(open, category, hasPendingQuestion)` is the ONE predicate both `buildAiRuntime` and handle-inbound's recording gate read** (trap 4): nothing renders on `opt_out` or while a knowledge-gap question is pending. A suppressed turn is burned, not the intention — nothing records, so it stays open.
  - **Recording.** The post-send classifier is retried once (`CLASSIFIER_ATTEMPTS = 2`); if both attempts fail, every RENDERED intention is closed with `prompt_source = 'pessimistic'`. The read already failed closed; a write that failed open was the asymmetry. `closed_pessimistically` and `write_failed` both fire `captureIntentionPromptRecordingFailed` (PostHog + Slack) **on every send path**, auto-send and operator dispatch alike (TAC-385 PR 1 added the dispatch half; before that it only `console.warn`ed, on the path where a pessimistic closure is MOST likely to be wrong). `agentRunId` is nullable for that reason — a queued draft's run ended when it was queued — and a required `via: 'auto_send' | 'operator_approve' | 'operator_edit'` says which path instead, so a fourth send path has to decide rather than inherit. Before this ticket a recording failure was a bare `console.warn`, and this ticket multiplies the intentions it applies to. **Every send path records, since TAC-385 PR 1.** An intention is ASKED when the message carrying it reaches the guest — auto-sent, operator-approved and operator-edited-then-sent alike (ruled 2026-09-15). `handle-inbound` records the auto-sent path; `dispatchOperatorOutbound` records the other two off `messages.rendered_intentions` (migration 045), the carrier the queue persist writes. Until then those sends recorded nothing: 13 of 34 sent replies at Le Mil's in the 30 days to 2026-09-14. **`renderableIntentions(...)` is called ONCE in `handle-inbound`, hoisted above the queue/send fork**, so what a card STORES and what an auto-send RECORDS are the same value by construction. **TAC-332's opener guard was applied there too until TAC-423 reversed it (ruled 2026-09-22): the opener turn now records like every other turn.** TAC-332 excluded it because the opener scripted its own question about whether the guest was new, so the classifier could only return a correct negative or a false positive that closes a one-shot goal forever. v1.52.0 inverted that premise by pointing the opener's question at `understand_order`, and v1.59.0 removed the scripted question altogether — what the opener turn now asks IS the first intention line, so refusing to record it was refusing to record the one ask that turn reliably makes. Measured before the change at Le Mil's: five guests enrolled by scanning, `understand_order` armed for every one and recorded as asked once. Because the guard sat on the one hoisted value, removing it lands both halves at once — the auto-send recording and the queued card's `rendered_intentions`. **Residual, accepted rather than assumed away:** `learn_name` is open on that turn too and the opener asks the model to say who the guest has reached. Introducing yourself is not asking someone's name and the classifier is told to omit anything it is unsure of, but if it false-positives, `learn_name` closes for that guest forever and silently, which is exactly what TAC-332 existed to prevent. The observable is a `learn_name` prompt recorded against an opener message whose text asks nothing about a name. The dispatch recorder is handed the **DISPATCHED body**, never `row.body` — that is the whole mechanism behind "read the ask from what was sent, not what was drafted": a question the operator edited OUT is simply not returned by the classifier. **Known limit, accepted:** a question the operator writes IN that the model never rendered cannot be returned either, because the key set is a per-call `z.enum` over the offered set; it stays open and may be asked again. **PR 1 changes nothing about WHEN an intention closes** — raising still closes, exactly as before; the asked/closed split is PR 2. The Command Center raised-prompts lists mark `prompt_source = 'pessimistic'` rows "closed without a verdict".
  - **Prompt (v1.49.0).** R31 gains a carve-out for asking how an item went — **only an item already in this guest's `## Visit history` or an open recommendation to them in `## Active commitments`, never any item the venue offers**; the broader version reopens exactly what TAC-356 closed. R32 lost its "the first-touch intentions block already covers it" clause, which became false when `invite_contact_save` retired. `their_rhythm` asks TIME OF DAY, never frequency: the R23 trip is the turn AFTER the question ("since you're in most mornings"), and no rewording rescues a goal that is about frequency. `definitions.test.ts` guards the wording.
  - Config lives on `venue_configs.intention_rules`; defaults are on `/admin/tunables`. `/admin/intentions` and the venue page's intentions section were reworked for state rows.

- **Intentions were never asked, and why (TAC-436, v1.51.0).** Between TAC-380 shipping and this, **zero intentions were ever raised in production**. They rendered and the model declined, and on 15 of 16 traced turns the block's own rules told it to. Two independent causes, both closed here.
  - **The prompt licensed the ask only in a situation that could not arise.** `formatOpenIntentions`' restraint paragraph carried six restraints and ONE concretely-worked permission — "when your own last message asked them something about themselves… and this reply answers it" — which presupposes an ask nothing else licensed. The deadlock in practice was one sentence, *"If the guest asks about something else, answer that and let these wait"*, which fired on all nine question turns of the sixteen. **That sentence is deleted** (ruling 1b: a reply may answer and then ask one small thing), and **four ordinary openings are now named positively** (ruling 1c) in place of the negation-only "a natural door". Every other restraint survives, one is new (an apology, bad news or an upset guest is never an opening), and `serializers.test.ts` carries a CANARY on the deleted sentence, because restoring it for brevity reverts the whole ticket silently. **Two deliberate omissions in the copy, both approved:** no em dash anywhere (the replaced text had two; R3 bans them in output and the prompt should not model them), and no emoji in the worked example (this block renders immediately before the per-message emoji call, so an example carrying one would argue with a `none` directive on ~25% of turns at a `frequent` venue).
  - **`comp_complaint` joins `opt_out` in BOTH `shouldRenderOpenIntentions` AND `renderableIntentions`** — the STRUCTURAL half of that new restraint, and it is what actually holds. **The two must move together and a test now enforces it across every category.** Suppressing on one side only does not leak a question into the reply, which is why it survived three commits of unit tests and was caught by the gate run: the block genuinely does not render, and the post-send classifier is still offered intentions the prompt never showed. The block renders LAST in the user prompt while `COMP_COMPLAINT_INSTRUCTIONS` lives in the SYSTEM prompt, so on proximity the block wins; the prose line is a second line of defence. Same pair `shouldRenderEmojiDirective` already excludes, the same TAC-314/329/330/338 failure class. Still not a claim these are the only two categories that should suppress it — no other has been audited.
  - **The bootstrap gap was arithmetic, not judgement.** `gateOpen` required `responseRate >= response_rate_floor`, and `normalizeResponseRate` returns 0 until three outbound responses exist against a floor defaulting to 50, so every conversational-gated intention was closed on a guest's first turns BY CONSTRUCTION, and the four first-contact intentions became eligible strictly after the only licence to raise them had expired. A third gate kind, **`replies_only`**, drops the floor and keeps the count. `gateOpen` is now an exhaustive switch, so a fourth kind fails `tsc`. **The waiver is declared PER INTENTION on its own gate, never inferred from `armsOn`** — arming and gating are orthogonal here on purpose, and nothing branches on `armsOn.kind` to decide a gate.
  - **`learn_name` alone is free on a guest's first-ever message** (`firstMessageMinReplies: 0`; ruled 2026-09-17, "explicit per intention, not a blanket zero"). The other three repeat their ongoing count there, which waives nothing, and say so explicitly so a new `replies_only` intention has to choose. NOT venue-overridable: `min_replies` tunes the ongoing stagger, not the opening exchange. "First-ever message" is read off `repliedMessageCount <= 1`, the same number the gate compares against, rather than a separately-plumbed flag that could drift from it — and deliberately NOT `recentMessages.length === 0`, which is a 14-day window and is also true for a guest returning after a long gap.
  - **`understand_order` arms on a CONFIRMED VISIT, not a QR scan** (`visit_confirmed` replaces `qr_scan_enrollment`). Two sources today, resolved by `build-runtime-context` and handed to the pure derivation as one date: `created_via = 'qr_scan'` anchored to enrollment, and the earliest `guest_commitments.acknowledged_at`. **The EARLIEST of them wins**, because the window runs from the anchor and this intention never re-arms, so a later visit must not renew an ask about the first order nobody heard. **`guests.last_visit_at` is DELIBERATELY NOT a source, and it is the one anyone reaches for first**: all three of its writers run downstream of a transaction row, and a transaction SATISFIES this intention, so arming on it would close the intention in the same breath it opened it. There is a source-level guard, matching both the snake_case column and the camelCase field — the first version matched only one and a mutant walked past it. A guest merely SAYING they came in, naming nothing they ordered, is recorded nowhere; that third source is TAC-386's and lands without touching `derive.ts` (ruled 2026-09-17). `DeriveOpenIntentionsInput.guest` was REMOVED in the same change rather than left dead, so a future `qr_scan` branch has to be added back deliberately instead of finding the field in scope.
  - **A scan on THIS TURN is a third confirmed-visit source (TAC-518), and it wins outright.** The two sources above are stamped once and never move, so neither can see a guest who has messaged the venue before and is at the pickup counter right now — on Instagram, exactly who the referral identifies. `buildRuntimeContext` reads `messages.referral_source` off the turn's own row through `isScanReferral` and uses the message's RECEIPT time as the anchor (`now` would move it later on a retried or delayed webhook). It OVERRIDES rather than joining `confirmedVisitTimes`, because that list is reduced with `Math.min` and the whole point is a LATER anchor; TAC-436's earliest-wins rule is untouched for the two historical sources and its reasoning still holds for them. **The boundary is the part to know before reading this as "a scan always re-arms": it does not re-arm `understand_order` for a guest who already has a row for it.** `rearmsOnNewerEvent` is false for `visit_confirmed`, so `derive.ts` skips any intention with an existing row whatever anchor it is handed. What this reaches is the guest who never had one — created by an ordinary DM, so `visitConfirmedAt` was null every turn until they scanned, which is the common shape at Le Mil's. Widening it further means reversing TAC-436 ruling 3 fleet-wide on both channels, which is its own decision and was deliberately not taken here. Both halves are pinned by tests, the boundary included, so it reads as a decision rather than a surprise. **SMS is unchanged by construction**: only the Instagram handler writes `referral_source`, so it is null on every Sendblue row and the historical resolution is what fires. **The opener is NOT wired to the referral** (ruled 2026-09-23, option A): a returning scanner gets order capture armed and no new prompt line, because the opener's text says "this is the guest's first message" and the wording for a returning guest is TAC-423's. A source-level test in `first-visit.test.ts` holds `computeFirstTouchAfterQrScan` free of the referral so that ruling cannot be undone by accident. **And the absence of a referral is made loud rather than inferred around**: `scanUnattributedReason` (pure, `handle-events.ts`) reports an inbound that looks like a scan and cannot prove it, as `instagram_scan_unattributed` (PostHog, Slack-relayed, emitted from the route through `waitUntil`). Two shapes qualify, both narrow: a POSTBACK with no referral, and a referral whose `source` is not the one meaning "opened from a link" — the only thing that would say so if Meta ever renamed that value. An ordinary message with no referral is deliberately NOT reported: that is a DM, and flagging it would fire on every organic inbound and therefore mean nothing, which is the `comp_regex_backstop` illusion again. **Be precise about what the postback case can and cannot see, because a first version of this entry was self-contradictory and code review caught it.** It sees Meta dropping the referral on the first-contact path that carries one today. It does NOT see the returning guest who opens the link into a thread that still has messages: `fixtures/README.md` records that such a thread shows no icebreakers, so there is no postback at all — that guest TYPES, and a typed message with no referral is indistinguishable from an ordinary DM. Device QA answers that case by reading `messages.referral_source` on the row, not by waiting for this event. It also has a known false positive, the likeliest first firing: a guest with no prior DM who finds the venue in search and taps an icebreaker. Read `guestCreated` beside it. **The POSITIVE half is `instagram_scan_confirmed_visit`** (`build-runtime-context.ts`), fired when a scan on this turn actually confirms a visit, Slack-relayed ONLY when the guest had prior messages. Without it a referral that DID arrive for a returning guest left no trace until the model happened to raise the line — and this repo has already had a stretch where no intention was raised in production, so that is not a signal to wait on. Both directions being observable is the point; **whether the returning-guest case delivers a referral at all is still UNKNOWN**, and if it turns out it does not, the ruling is to say so and stop rather than infer a scan from something weaker.
  - **`rendered_intentions` is written on the auto-send path too** (ruling 4), on the FIRST row of a split turn only — one prompt, one rendered set, so a count of non-null rows counts responses rather than bubbles. **AUDIT, NOT MECHANISM**: that path records inline and nothing downstream reads the column there. It exists so a query can prove what rendered, which is precisely what TAC-385's raising-half audit could not do — every auto-sent row carried NULL and its claim about those turns was inference. `handle-inbound` passes the SAME hoisted value to both the queue and send branches, so a card and an auto-send cannot drift.
  - **A successful raise now emits `intention_prompt_raised`** (ruling 5) to PostHog and Slack, from all three send paths, carrying `via`, the raised keys, the OFFERED keys and the sent body. Until this it was a bare `console.log`, which is why "nothing has ever been raised" was invisible for the feature's whole life. `offeredKeys` is the RENDERED set, never `ctx.openIntentions`, so the event can never claim a door was open that the turn suppressed; without it a 1-of-4 raise is indistinguishable from a 1-of-1. Slack-relayed deliberately at pilot volume: the question it exists to answer is "has an intention ever been raised", and at this rate the relay IS the answer.
  - **Known and NOT fixed here:** the first-touch opener is still QR-only (`computeFirstTouchAfterQrScan`), so a guest who texts the number without scanning gets no introduction — most guests on file. Ruling 3 widens ARMING, not the licence; ruling 1's rewrite is what makes the line askable on an ordinary turn, so the two only work together. Widening the opener is its own ticket (ruled 2026-09-17, audit question 3).

- **Instagram outbound (TAC-469).** A reply picks its transport in ONE place, `dispatchReply` (`lib/agent/dispatch-reply.ts`), an exhaustive switch on `ctx.conversationChannel`: `'text'` is `scheduleAndSend` exactly as it was (throws included; the existing text tests run through it unchanged), `'instagram'` is `dispatchInstagramReply` (`lib/agent/dispatch-instagram-reply.ts`), and **nothing routes on null**: `handleInbound` stops a null-channel run before classifying (red alert, `failed`), after `buildRuntimeContext` has raised `conversation_channel_unresolved` to PostHog and Slack. **Branch by channel, don't converge**: the window, the byte cap and the reply check live only on the Instagram side, and `lib/messaging/instagram/window-import-guard.test.ts` fails if anything else imports them or if the Instagram arms import the Sendblue transport or the phone lookup. The rules, each ruled on the ticket (2026-09-19):
  - **Outbound splits by origin.** A reply to something the guest just did (an inbound reply, the crisis-safety reply, the knowledge-gap holding message, an operator-approved card) may go out over the API. **A follow-up never auto-sends on Instagram**, whatever the window says: `handleFollowup` refuses an Instagram conversation (and an unresolved one) before generating, demo guests included, and the Command Center Follow Up button refuses it by channel before the venue-number check.
  - **The window is a guard, not a router**, computed from `provider_sent_at` (Meta's clock) on the newest Instagram inbound row that has one, never `created_at` (measured 1.8s and 2.3s later, far more on a redelivery). `INSTAGRAM_WINDOW_MARGIN_MS` is 5 minutes, a judgment: the known error left after reading Meta's time is clock skew plus the send timeout, about 11s. `instagram_send_failed` carries `windowRemainingMs`, so a Meta refusal (subcode 2534022) on a send the gate passed would show the margin wrong. An unreadable window sends anyway and lets Meta decide.
  - **The 1000-byte cap** (UTF-8 bytes, not characters) is refused by the transport and never truncated. The agent arm keeps replies under it by repacking whole sentences across up to three messages; a reply it can't repack is not sent at all and becomes a card. An operator's text is sent verbatim, so an over-cap card is refused before it leaves the queue.
  - **The reply check**: an outbound row sent after guest message X answers X when it names no inbound (every reply staff type in the Instagram app) or names X or a later inbound; a reply naming an EARLIER message does not (the oat-milk case: without that exception the agent would silence its own second answer, a bug Sendblue doesn't have). Compared on Meta's clock when both rows have it, else ours: for an outbound row that is `sent_at`, falling back to `created_at` only when it has none, because a card is created long before it is sent. **The crisis-safety reply is exempt** and always sends. A silenced reply is `AgentResult` status `superseded`; the holding message maps it to `suppressed: 'answered_by_hand'`. Known race, not engineered around: an echo arriving within about 2s of our send is missed.
  - **The echo can arrive before the Send API answers.** The agent arm inserts after sending; a collision on `messages_provider_message_id_unique` means the echo landed first, and it fills in that echo row (matched on the mid, the guest, outbound, `generated_by` null), keeping the echo's body and `provider_sent_at`. The operator arm's card row already exists and is referenced, so it FOLDS the echo in: copies the echo's `provider_sent_at` onto the card, deletes the echo row, then writes the mid (`lib/operator/dispatch-instagram-outbound.ts`). That is the first code path that deletes a `messages` row, guarded to that one echo. **When our write lands first, the echo handler skips the duplicate and the row keeps `provider_sent_at` NULL**, so no reader may assume an outbound Instagram row has it.
  - **A send that fails becomes a card, never a retry loop.** The whole reply (with its commitment carrier and rendered intentions) or the unsent remainder of a split one is persisted with `review_reason = 'instagram_send_failed'` under the `never_regen` slot rule, and `handleInbound` fires the push, on the crisis path too (orchestrators fire pushes; a helper that did would pull the push module into every path that imports it). **A card is not always possible**: a guest who opted out gets none, and neither does a reply whose slot a knowledge-gap card already holds, since overwriting it would destroy the operator's question. Both are named on the Slack event, which carries the undelivered text either way. `captureInstagramSendFailed` Slack-relays the undelivered text, including when no card could be written. The holding message writes no card: its knowledge-gap card already holds the guest's place. On the operator path a send Meta definitely refused puts the card back in the queue; an unknown outcome (timeout, network, an unreadable 200) stays out, as on Sendblue, because it may already be in the thread. The approve and edit routes map every new code to the existing 502 body with a plain-words `detail`, so the operator API Contract is unchanged.
  - **A guest with both identifiers** is, on a run with no inbound message, on the channel they last messaged us on (`resolveConversationChannel`'s `lastInboundChannel`), so copy and routing read one answer.
  - **A row that names no inbound answers everything before it**, so anything the agent sends ON INSTAGRAM must name what it answers (the Sendblue holding row still names nothing, and nothing on that channel reads it): the holding message passes `answersInboundId`, on every message of a split one (its context has no `currentMessage`, so the row would otherwise name nothing and silence the agent's reply to a question asked while it was being written). The operator-decline card still names nothing; it is a card, so it only reaches the check once an operator sends it.
  - No read receipt or typing indicator is ever sent for an Instagram message (Sendblue's would go to the guest's phone; Meta's sender actions are not built).

- **A guest's burst is one turn, and exactly one run may reply (TAC-526).** Both webhooks call `waitUntil(runInboundAgent(id))` once per inbound row, so two messages seconds apart start two independent runs in two serverless invocations that share no memory. Live at Le Mil's on 2026-09-23: 7 seconds between the guest's two messages, 5 between the two replies, and the guest was asked their name twice. Measured frequency at the time: 37 of 168 outbound messages went out within 30 seconds of the previous outbound to the same guest, 87 within two minutes (follow-ups and operator sends are in that number, so it is an upper bound, not a rate). **Gated by `INBOUND_COALESCING_ENABLED` (`lib/agent/coalesce-turn.ts`), TAC-469 PR C's shape: the flip is its own one-line commit so a rollback is a one-line revert.**
  **The correction that decides the design, and it is the most important line here.** The ticket said each run was generated without knowledge of the other. That is half wrong. Both runs could see the other's MESSAGE — `build-runtime-context.ts` excludes only `currentMessage.id`, so the second run had the first message in `## Recent conversation`, rendered `[just now]`. Neither could see the other's REPLY, because it did not exist yet. So the fix is **"only one run may produce a reply"**, not "let the reply see both messages" — which is why context assembly is untouched, no prompt file is edited, and `PROMPT_VERSION` is not bumped.
  **Three mechanisms, in the order a turn meets them.** (1) **Settle** — wait `COALESCE_SETTLE_MS` before claiming, so a fragment already in flight lands before a model call is spent. (2) **Claim** — exactly one run per `(venue_id, guest_id)` proceeds; the loser records itself and exits. (3) **Extension** — the winner re-checks immediately before dispatch and adopts a message that arrived while it generated, bounded by `MAX_TURN_EXTENSIONS` (2). **The run that wakes first claims and answers the NEWEST message it can see**, rather than deferring to the later run: deferring makes the guest wait the later run's settle too and leaves a window where nobody holds the turn.
  **The window is 8 seconds and the trade is written down because it is a real cost.** The observed gap was 7s. But TAC-421 deleted a 6.5s pre-send sleep for being 27% of a 24.4s first-bubble p50, and this adds 8s back; the difference is what the delay buys — TAC-421's sleep bought nothing (its own invariant test was a tautology) and this buys one reply instead of two. **The no-settle alternative was costed and rejected, not overlooked:** at `COALESCE_SETTLE_MS = 0` every acceptance criterion still passes, because the pre-dispatch extension catches what the settle misses. Against the ticket's own 22% burst rate, no-settle is **~5s better in expectation** (21.3s vs 26s), **~7s worse per burst** (~33s vs ~26s), and spends **one wasted generation set per burst** (~0.22 per turn). So 8s trades expected latency for worst-case latency and model cost; the lever is one constant and `scripts/measurement/coalesce-window.ts` is what supplies evidence to move it. **Also on the latency ledger: the read receipt fires inside `scheduleAndSend`, so the settle delays it by the same 8s.** Firing it earlier was considered and is out of scope.
  **The post-turn handoff is not an optimisation — it is what stops the claim being a robustness regression.** Today two runs is the bug and also the redundancy: if run A dies, run B still replies. Add a claim and remove the handoff and run B has already exited as a loser, so the guest gets silence. `closeCoalescedTurn` releases the claim and then, if an inbound newer than what this turn answered still exists, re-invokes `handleInbound` for it — and if there is NOTHING newer but the turn failed, re-invokes for the message it answered instead, once (see `MAX_TURN_RETRIES` below). Those two are mutually exclusive by construction and together they are what keep the claim from costing a guest their reply. **`findUncoveredInbound` is THREE-state and the third is load-bearing**: it returned `null` for both "nothing newer" and "the read failed", which is the right fail-open direction for the EXTENSION (send what you have) and exactly backwards for the HANDOFF, where it meant no handoff at all — so a single transient `messages` read silenced a folded message permanently, with no retry and nothing logged. Its own docstring asserted the opposite. An unreadable check now logs at error level and fires `inbound_turn_handoff_check_failed`; it cannot be recovered from there (a retry needs the id the read failed to produce), so the obligation is to make it visible rather than to guess. It runs on **every** terminal path including the wrapper's top-level catch, which is why it lives in `handleInbound` rather than the orchestrator — the orchestrator's own `finally` cannot see a throw that escaped it. **It is dead code on the happy path, which is exactly the problem**: a future reader who sees "release the claim, then maybe re-invoke" will delete the re-invoke as unreachable. It is reachable on a throw, an exhausted extension budget, a refusal, a drop and a queue. **Release happens BEFORE the handoff**, or the handed-off run loses the claim it was invoked to take.
  **"Never throws" was a claim in a docstring and was FALSE until the flag was flipped.** supabase-js surfaces most failures as `{ error }` but THROWS on some (an unreachable host, a malformed client), and an escaping throw lands in `runInboundTurn`'s top-level catch and fails the whole turn — fail-CLOSED, a guest silenced because a claim table hiccuped, the exact inversion this module exists to avoid. `claimInboundTurn`, `releaseInboundTurn` and `findUncoveredInbound` each catch now, and a throw from the newest-message read is `unreadable` rather than `none` so it cannot reintroduce the handoff blocker by another route. **None of the 30 mutants found it**: a type cannot express "does not throw", so only a test can, and the one that exposed it was the whole existing orchestrator suite going red the moment the constant changed. **Everything fails OPEN.** A store that cannot be read or written returns `unavailable` and the run proceeds exactly as it does today, unclaimed, with a `console.warn`. Blocking a reply because a claim table was unreachable would make a guest's silence a NEW failure mode introduced by the fix for a duplicate reply.
  **The boundary with TAC-397 is clean and neither mechanism is duplicated.** A run in progress is this ticket's claim; a draft already waiting for an operator is TAC-397's `resolveConversationDisposition`, which is untouched. Concretely: **the extension fires only on the auto-send path, never the queue path** — a queued turn releases its claim and TAC-397 owns what the next message does.
  **Crisis-safety never extends, and that is structural rather than a check** — the crisis short-circuit returns hundreds of lines before the extension, so a fixed unconditional reply can never be deferred to a newer fragment. A crisis message arriving SECOND is still answered, by the winner that adopted it; if extensions are exhausted, the handoff covers it. There is a test pinning that a crisis turn never reaches the extension.
  **The claiming message's row carries the turn's outcome.** a message folded into that turn gets `outcome: 'superseded'` with `reason: 'coalesced_into_turn'` and `detail.coalescedIntoAgentRunId`; an extension writes no extra row (same run, same claim, same `agentRunId`, which is why the extension RE-ENTERS `runInboundTurn` rather than calling `handleInbound` afresh). **It is NOT one row per inbound message, and a first version of this entry claimed it was**: a message whose own run stood down records `coalesced_into_turn`, and if the winner then queues (no extension on the queue path) and hands that same message off, the handed-off run records a SECOND terminal row for it. That is consistent with precedent rather than a defect — migration 055's header already says there is no unique constraint and a second event is a real second row, and `skipped_duplicate` carries exactly the same meaning — but the sentence was wrong. `AgentResult` gains a `coalesced` member — **a separate member rather than a field on `superseded`**, whose own docstring says a reply already existed, which is false here; reusing it would make that comment false, and the separate member is what makes the ledger's total map refuse to compile until someone decides what it records. With `skipped_duplicate` it is the second value meaning the agent ran more than once for one guest action, so a strict turn count is `where layer = 'agent' and outcome <> 'skipped_duplicate' and reason is distinct from 'coalesced_into_turn'`.
  **Latency is emitted once per turn, by the outermost call only** (`entryExtensionDepth === 0`, captured at entry because an extension increments the counter before recursing). Both calls emitting would double-count one turn; the outermost elapsed covers the settle and every extension, which is the number worth having.
  **THE CLAIM WOULD HAVE BEEN A ROBUSTNESS REGRESSION, and the retry is what stops it (found in code review, ruled 2026-09-23).** Before this ticket two runs were the bug AND the redundancy: if the winner died the loser still replied, about seven seconds later, with its own embed, classify and generate calls. The claim removes the loser — so when the winner adopts the newest message and then FAILS, there is nothing newer to hand off and the loser has already stood down. Two chances became one, on roughly the 22% of turns that are bursts, and the failure mode is a guest receiving nothing. **`MAX_TURN_RETRIES = 1` restores the second attempt and nothing more**, fired from `closeCoalescedTurn` only when `findUncoveredInbound` says `none` — a newer message already gets a fresh run that covers the conversation, so the retry and the handoff are mutually exclusive by construction. **Bounded by a DEPTH threaded into the re-invocation, not a counter**, because the retry is a fresh `handleInbound` and a counter local to a run cannot bound something that starts a new run; without it a deterministically failing turn re-invokes itself forever, spending a model call each time. `RETRYABLE_OUTCOME` is a total `satisfies Record<AgentResult['status'], boolean>` map so a new member fails `tsc` until someone decides. `failed` and `refused` retry, because on both the guest gets nothing; a THROW retries too, being the strongest case. **`dropped` deliberately does NOT, and it is the exclusion worth arguing** — the guest gets nothing there as well, but a draft that lost a slot loses it again on a second attempt, since the card that took the slot is still there, so a retry is a guaranteed-useless second generation rather than a second chance. **Known and NOT fixed here:** a function killed outright (OOM, wall-clock) runs no code, so nothing retries or hands off and the claim sits until its lease expires — already true today for a single message, now recorded by TAC-523. **The handoff chain also runs inside the original invocation's `waitUntil` budget** and no `maxDuration` is declared on either webhook route, so a long burst chains settle-plus-turn serially in one invocation; worth measuring before the flip rather than assuming. The history query's `.neq('body', '')` means a **media-only fragment** in a burst is invisible to the prompt, and history bodies are truncated for rendering; neither is introduced here and neither is fixed here. Followups, operator sends and the holding message are not coalesced — inbound only.

### Approval policy gates (TAC-212, v1.14.0)

`applyApprovalPolicyStage` (`lib/agent/stages.ts`) runs immediately after a successful `generateStage` on both the inbound and followup orchestrators. It returns `{ action: 'send' }` or `{ action: 'queue', triggers, primaryTrigger, compMatchedPattern, existingPendingDraftId }`. On `queue`, the orchestrator calls `persistOrRegenQueuedDraft` (`lib/agent/schedule-and-send.ts`) — same row shape as `scheduleAndSend` via the shared `buildOutboundInsert` helper, but with `status='pending_review'`, `review_state='pending'` (TAC-258 migration 018 predicate), `review_reason=<primaryTrigger>`, `sent_at=null`, `provider_message_id=null`. No Sendblue dispatch. The `AgentResult.queued` discriminated-union member carries `outboundMessageId`, `triggers`, and `primaryTrigger`. **TAC-350 adds a third, optional parameter** — `applyApprovalPolicyStage(ctx, generation, groundingBackstop?)` — carrying the result of `verifyGroundingStage`, which the orchestrator must run (it needs an async AI call the gate itself can't make mid-evaluation) and pass in; omitted or `null` behaves exactly as before TAC-350. **TAC-355 adds a fourth, optional parameter** — `applyApprovalPolicyStage(ctx, generation, groundingBackstop?, mechanicOfferBackstop?)` — carrying the result of `verifyMechanicOfferStage`, run by the orchestrator alongside `verifyGroundingStage` via `Promise.all` (both are independent Haiku calls with no dependency on each other). Omitted defaults to `{ status: 'skipped' }`, behaving exactly as before TAC-355.

**Twenty-three triggers compose; any one queues** — the count matches `APPROVAL_TRIGGERS`' members, which is the thing to check it against. Enumeration order (the order the gate evaluates and the order they appear in `triggers[]`):
1. `fidelity_below_auto_send_floor` — `voiceFidelity` in `[0.4, 0.6)`. (`< 0.4` is already refused upstream.)
2. `model_flagged` — `GeneratedMessageSchema.requiresOperatorApproval=true`. Reason is in `GenerateMessageResult.approvalReason`. Two prompt triggers teach the model when to flag: the universal comp rule in `# Resource commitment self-flag` (`SYSTEM_TEMPLATE`), and per-mechanic instructions appended to flagged-mechanic bullets in `formatMechanicEligibility`.
3. `comp_regex_backstop` — `matchComp` (`lib/agent/comp-backstop.ts`) hits a high-precision operator-action regex. Runs **independently** of `model_flagged` — when the model misses a self-flag on a comp, the regex still queues. False positives are acceptable; false negatives are the failure mode this exists to prevent.
4. `previous_pending_held` — **since TAC-397, fires ONLY on a CORRECTION**, i.e. exactly when the persist layer is about to overwrite a card in place, which is the one case where the label is true. For the obligation slot it still fires on any same-slot occupant (TAC-394 unchanged). Before TAC-397 it fired on any occupied slot, and TAC-394's QA (2026-09-21) established it was **false every single time it rendered**: same-slot occupancy forced a regen or a drop, never an insert, so the row carrying "Held behind an earlier message to this guest" was always the row that message had just replaced, and the operator was told to clear something that no longer existed. Copy approved 2026-09-22: *"You updated this after the guest wrote again. Check it still answers everything."* — and the 2026-09-15 ruling on this label is **superseded** (it approved wording for the trigger's TAC-394 meaning). **The consequence is the headline behaviour change of TAC-397: a clean answer to a guest's SECOND question now AUTO-SENDS where it used to queue**, because an occupied slot is no longer a trigger on its own; it still passes every other gate on its own merits. **Fails OPEN** on DB error: `loadPendingRowsBySlot` throws or errors → returns `null` → the gate proceeds as if nothing is pending. Migration 054's index (which replaced 041's conversation half) is the structural backstop against concurrent rapid-inbound races that slip past this fail-open read.
5. `commitment_type_gated` (TAC-297) — `GeneratedMessageSchema.commitment.type ∈ {comp, hold, discount}` AND `description` non-empty. Fires regardless of `requiresOperatorApproval` self-flag — the structured emission IS the backstop (TAC-297 design call #2). Recommendation type does NOT fire this trigger. **The comp regex stays as belt-and-suspenders** for prose-comp-without-emission cases the model might produce.
6. `hold_all_outbound` (commit `0c1515c`, migration 031) — `ctx.venue.holdAllOutbound === true` AND `ctx.classification?.category !== 'opt_out'`. Per-venue blanket hold: every guest-facing content message is queued for review. The opt_out carve-out is a TCPA/carrier requirement — compliance confirmations must auto-send — and it bypasses ONLY this trigger; an opt_out reply still runs triggers 1–5. Composes with (does not short-circuit) the others, so `existingPendingDraftId` still routes regen-in-place correctly. **No UI or API writes this flag** — `venues.hold_all_outbound` is Studio-SQL-only, like `guests.is_demo` and `operators.is_analog_admin`; SQL template in Common gotchas.

7. `complaint_commitment_floor` (v1.23.0) — `ctx.classification.category` is in `FLOOR_CATEGORIES` (today: `comp_complaint` only) AND `matchForwardCommitment(body)` hits first-person forward-commitment grammar (`lib/agent/complaint-floor.ts`). **Deterministic: does not read `requiresOperatorApproval` or `commitment` at all.** That independence is the entire point — on 2026-08-07 the model reported both empty and the reply still gave away free product on a refund request. Gates on promise GRAMMAR, not remedy vocabulary, because the set of ways to say "I commit to a future action" is small and closed while the set of ways to describe what's being given is unbounded. Measured against the complete production history of `comp_complaint` outbounds: 8/12 queue, 6 true positives, 2 accepted false positives (prompt-endorsed information stalls), all pure-question turns pass through. Scope is `comp_complaint` ONLY — `mechanic_request` is deliberately excluded so ordinary perk refusals ("can i get a free drink") can never be held.

9. `knowledge_gap` (TAC-308) — `GeneratedMessageSchema.knowledgeGap === true` AND `ctx.currentMessage !== null`. The model answered a guest question it could not ground in venue knowledge. **The only trigger that starts a clock**, and since TAC-484 only when `ctx.currentMessage` reads as a question (`looksLikeQuestion`): the queue persist stamps `messages.pending_until = now + KNOWLEDGE_GAP_WINDOW_MS` (5 min). **Nothing then sends anything** — TAC-484 disabled the timer's holding message (`KNOWLEDGE_GAP_HOLDING_MESSAGE_ENABLED`), so the stamp is currently inert and the card simply waits for an operator. Before TAC-484 the cron sent the guest a model-generated holding message when the window elapsed. Inbound-only — a followup has no guest question outstanding, and letting a cron-triggered proactive message arm a clock would produce a holding note for something nobody asked.

9b. `knowledge_gap_backstop` (TAC-350) — independent grounding backstop, fired from `groundingBackstop.status === 'flagged'` (TAC-367 shape; was `!== null` before that widening — see the new third parameter above). Exists because trigger 9 is pure self-report and an audit of a real TAC-347 harness run found 8/8 observed fabrications had `knowledgeGap=false` — the model confidently invented a wifi password, four menu-item variation names, and other specifics with no structural check ever comparing the claim against what was actually retrieved. `verifyGroundingStage` (`lib/agent/stages.ts`) closes that gap with a second, independent Haiku call (`lib/ai/verify-grounding.ts`) that inspects the drafted body against the SAME `venueInfo` + `knowledgeChunks` the generator saw and reports any claim not supported by them — same relationship `comp_regex_backstop` has to `model_flagged`. **Only ever invoked when trigger 9 is already false** (no point re-checking a self-reported gap), so the two are mutually exclusive on any single turn by construction. Shares trigger 9's clock arming and protected-card carve-out via the `isGapTurn = knowledgeGapFired || backstopFired` union inside the gate, and `isKnowledgeGapCard` recognizes both `review_reason` values — but **NOT body blanking**, which TAC-301 part 1.5 made the one asymmetry between them (self-report blanks, backstop keeps its body; see below). **TAC-301 part 1.5 fixed three defects in this backstop that together made it fire on CORRECT replies.** (1) **The verifier was missing the entire runtime context.** `buildSourceMaterial` was `venueInfo` + `knowledgeChunks` only, so every fact the generator drew from a runtime block read as unsupported — measured against Le Mil's live config, SIX of six fact-bearing blocks produced a false flag (`## Right now`, `## What this guest can access`, `## Active commitments`, `## Visit history`, `## Guest context`, `## Recent conversation`). It now receives `generation.userPrompt` **verbatim** — the literal string the generating model got, available on `GenerateMessageResult` since THE-216. **Never rebuild or curate that string**: a hand-maintained subset falls behind the next runtime block, which is exactly how all six arrived (TAC-296/297/308/324 each appended one). (2) **`reasoning` was declared LAST in the output schema**, and structured-output fields generate in declaration order, so the model emitted its verdict before doing the analysis; a reply naming the guest's last order produced reasoning that reversed itself and ended "This IS supported... The claim is grounded" while the boolean stayed `true`. `reasoning` is now FIRST and **the order is load-bearing**. (3) **The verifier exceeded its remit** three ways, each flagging a correct reply: re-litigating whether a guest QUALIFIES for a perk (eligibility is already decided by `filterEligibleMechanics` before the block renders), flagging hedged phrasing about a fact that IS in the source material, and judging whether saying something was wise. The system prompt now scopes it to factual support only. **`blankBody` no longer fires on this trigger** — see the reversal note below. Verified behaviourally, not just by unit test: all six divergences plus four controls (fabricated password, perk not on the list, eligibility-is-not-a-reservation, and the agent's own prior fabrication) pass against live calls, 7 of 8 full runs clean with one unidentified single-case flake. **Fails CLOSED on every failure since TAC-424, after one immediate retry on a transient fault** (truncation is not retried). It failed OPEN on transient faults from TAC-350 until then, with truncation carved out as fail-closed by TAC-367 — see trigger 12 for what overturned the fail-open half and why the retry is what makes the closed posture affordable. PostHog: `captureUngroundedClaimCaught` (`lib/analytics/posthog.ts`), Slack-relayed, fired from inside `verifyGroundingStage` — distinct from the generic `draft_queued` event so "how often is the model caught fabricating, per venue" is directly queryable. **`verifyGroundingStage` no longer returns `GroundingBackstopFinding | null`** — TAC-367 widened it to a four-state `GroundingBackstopResult` (`skipped | clean | flagged | truncated`) mirroring TAC-355's `MechanicOfferBackstopResult`, because a two-state shape had nowhere to put "we could not read the verdict" that was distinguishable from "there was nothing to report." `null` is still accepted at the gate and normalized to `skipped`.

8. `category_requires_approval` (v1.24.0; **made absolute by TAC-307**) — `resolvePolicyDecision(venue.approvalPolicy, classification.category)` returns `'operator_approval'`. **The only trigger decided by the CLASSIFICATION rather than the draft**, which is what makes it knowable before generation and lets the prompt be comp-forward (see `willBeReviewed` below).

   **The clarifying-question carve-out is now SUBORDINATE to the policy, not parallel to it.** It used to run alongside the policy check (`policy === 'operator_approval' && !canAutoSendComplaintTurn(...)`), which meant a turn the model labelled `clarifying` could auto-send THROUGH a hold an operator had deliberately switched on. The line is drawn on **who chose the hold**, via `PolicyDecision.source`:
   - source `stored` (an explicit `perCategory` entry on this venue) or `policy_default` (this venue's own `default`) → **ABSOLUTE**. `canAutoSendComplaintTurn` is not consulted at all.
   - source `code_default` (`APPROVAL_POLICY_DEFAULT.perCategory`, which ships fleet-wide and nobody chose per venue) → the carve-out still applies, because stalling a complaint's opening "what went wrong?" behind an operator is worse service than the cold reply v1.24.0 shipped to fix.

   Every venue in production stores `perCategory: {}`, so this is a **no-op against current behaviour** — and the moment a category is ticked in Command Center it becomes strictly stronger than the default it replaced. A venue-level `default: 'operator_approval'` is checked BEFORE the code-level `perCategory` map on purpose: without that ordering the master switch would not be absolute for `comp_complaint`, the one category that has a code default of its own — the hole hiding in exactly the category this ticket's incident was about.

   **`willBeReviewed` is scoped to complaint categories (TAC-307).** `buildAiRuntime`'s flag used to be "policy holds this category", full stop, which was harmless while a venue-wide `default: 'operator_approval'` needed hand-written SQL and no venue had one. This ticket ships a master switch that sets exactly that, and an unscoped flag would turn `formatMechanicEligibility`'s comp-forward branch on for EVERY turn at a holding venue — the agent proposing to make it up to a guest who asked whether the cafe is open. It now additionally requires `isFloorCategory(category)`. Guaranteed review is a necessary condition for inviting generosity, never a sufficient one.

   **`POLICY_EXEMPT_CATEGORIES` (TAC-307) beats everything above.** Today: `opt_out` only. TCPA/carrier compliance — an opt-out confirmation must reach the guest unconditionally, so it can never be routed to approval whatever a venue stores, an admin clicks, or someone hand-writes in Studio. **Enforced in the resolver, not the UI**, because hand-editing `venue_configs` is a normal workflow here and an exclusion guarded only by a rendering decision is not guarded. The Command Center surface reads the same constant to omit the control, and the write route refuses it independently. This mirrors the carve-out migration 031 already has on the `hold_all_outbound` axis (trigger 6, `category !== 'opt_out'`) — the two are now symmetric.

9c. `unverified_url` (TAC-509) — a link in the reply is not on the venue's curated `venue_info.links` allowlist and survived every regen attempt. Deterministic, unconditional, never a send. Enumerated here by TAC-424 only because that ticket touched the count above and found this one missing from the list; see the fuller entry under *A link in a reply must be on the venue's curated list* in the runtime contract.
10. `self_talk_detected` (TAC-355) — `GenerateMessageResult.selfTalkViolationPersisted === true`. Deterministic, unconditional — fires whenever the agent's own self-correction or reference to its instructions/rules/AI-nature survived every regen attempt inside `generateMessage`'s loop (`lib/ai/self-talk-detector.ts`, wired alongside `DASH_REGEX`, sharing its attempt budget). **Never a send, unlike the dash case** — THE-225 ships a persistent dash anyway (punctuation isn't worth refusing over); a guest reading agent self-talk learns they're texting a bot, which is categorical harm regardless of rate, so this trigger always queues instead. No body-blanking, no clock — the operator card already renders the full draft body, so the broken text is directly visible for them to edit.

11. `mechanic_offer_backstop` (TAC-355) — independent verification backstop for the mechanic-approval gate, fired from `mechanicOfferBackstop.status === 'flagged' || 'check_failed'` (the new fourth parameter — see below). Exists because trigger 2 (`model_flagged`) and trigger 5 (`commitment_type_gated`) both missed a real approval-gated mechanic grant (Referral Surprise, `le-mils-coffee`): audited and confirmed structural — nothing in the prompt links a mechanic grant from `## What this guest can access` to `commitment.type`, and a mechanic's reward can be genuinely non-nameable (`"exact item at staff discretion"`) or not a product at all (an event-invite-type mechanic), so the vocabulary has no bucket for it regardless of how faithfully the model tries. **This is the PRIMARY mechanism for that failure mode, not a secondary layer** — unlike `comp_regex_backstop`'s relationship to `model_flagged`, a regex on mechanic name/reward text was evaluated and rejected (mechanic identifying text is per-venue free prose, not a closed vocabulary; see the TAC-355 audit trail on the ticket). `verifyMechanicOfferStage` (`lib/agent/stages.ts`) runs a second, independent Haiku call (`lib/ai/verify-mechanic-offer.ts`) against the SAME eligible-`requires_operator_approval`-mechanics bullets the generator saw. Skips (no model call) when nothing gated is eligible this turn (the common case), when trigger 2 or 5 already fired (`isModelFlagged`/`isCommitmentTypeGated`, extracted so this skip check can't drift from the trigger's own push logic), or for a demo guest. **FAILS CLOSED** — a `check_failed` result (errored/timed out/unparseable) queues exactly like a confirmed `flagged` result. That was the deliberate opposite of `knowledge_gap_backstop`'s posture until TAC-424 closed the gap; the reasoning behind it stands on its own and did not depend on the contrast: an unauthorized perk grant costs the owner money and control, a failed check costs one unnecessary review. Runs on BOTH inbound and followup paths — a mechanic can be offered on a proactive outbound exactly as easily as in reply — and, since TAC-376, grounding runs on the same set of paths too (plus the holding message), so the two backstops no longer differ on REACH. Since TAC-424 the failure posture no longer differs either: all three post-generation checks fail CLOSED after one retry on a transient fault. What this one still does that grounding does not is fold `flagged` and `check_failed` under ONE trigger code, where grounding splits the cause across `grounding_check_failed` and `grounding_check_degraded`. PostHog: `captureMechanicOfferBackstopCaught`, Slack-relayed, fired only on a confirmed `flagged` result (not on `check_failed`).

12. `grounding_check_failed` (TAC-367, **widened by TAC-424**) — the grounding backstop did not produce a readable verdict. **Two causes now, both fail CLOSED, one trigger.** TAC-367 shipped it for TRUNCATION only (`finishReason: 'length'`, the output cap cut the JSON off mid-object), as a narrowing of trigger 9b's otherwise fail-open posture. **TAC-424 reversed the fail-open half**: a TRANSIENT fault (network, provider 5xx, timeout) that survives one immediate retry now fires this trigger too, so the draft is held rather than sent. Measured on Le Mil's live config: 12 paced calls on a production-size prompt (13,299 chars / 5,673 input tokens) produced 11 successes emitting **373–496 output tokens against a 500 cap** — the best success cleared it by four tokens — and one truncation. Every truncation failed open with no PostHog and no Slack, so the only fabrication check that fires under real traffic was silently not running on a slice of inbound turns. Same `MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` schema-growth hazard CLAUDE.md documents for TAC-309, arriving by a different route: TAC-301 part 1.5 moved unbounded `reasoning` ahead of the verdict, which is load-bearing for CORRECTNESS and must stay, but put the long field first against a cap that never moved. `VERIFY_GROUNDING_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is now 2000 — headroom, not a bound, since `reasoning` is still unbounded; the fail-closed handling is what actually closes the hole. **Transient faults used to fail OPEN, and no longer do (TAC-424, ruled 2026-09-21).** The old reasoning was that grounding runs on every inbound, so queuing every provider hiccup closed would be a fleet-wide queue flood. What overturned it: TAC-401's prose-promise check now runs CONCURRENTLY on nearly every generation and already fails closed after one retry, so during an outage the reply is held regardless — failing open here bought no availability at all and left the one path where an invented fact could reach a guest unchecked. **The retry is what pays for the closed posture**: the flood case narrows from a single Haiku blip to a fault that survives two immediate attempts, which is an outage rather than a hiccup. Truncation is deliberately NOT retried — retrying a cap that was already hit spends a second call to hit it again, and the fix is the cap. **A DISTINCT trigger rather than reusing `knowledge_gap_backstop`**, even though `mechanic_offer_backstop` sets the opposite precedent by covering both `flagged` and `check_failed` under one code — reusing it would tell the operator "ungrounded claim caught" for a turn where nothing was caught, a third instance of the wrong-reason-copy problem TAC-364 exists for. **Deliberately NOT part of `isGapTurn`, on either cause**: an incomplete check is an absence of information about the reply, not a finding against it, and everything keyed on `isGapTurn` has a guest-facing consequence that would be wrong here — arming `pending_until` puts a holding message in front of a guest whose reply was probably fine, and the protected-card carve-out silently DROPS the guest's next turn if that turn queues for any other reason. It queues the draft for a human to glance at; that is the whole intended consequence. **But it IS part of `checkDidNotComplete`, and that pairing is the trap** — the drop exemption is a separate expression from `isGapTurn`, and TAC-424 had to add `degraded` to it in the same change that added the trigger. Without it, a guest already holding a knowledge-gap card gets silence the next time the verifier faults twice: the new trigger makes `triggers.length > 0`, which cancels the carve-out. TAC-367 hit the identical shape for truncation. A record-keeping ticket would have shipped a guest-facing regression.
